The house resumed, from Monday, October 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for an address to His Majesty the King praying that a measure be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to amend the British North America Act, 1867, relating to the amendment of the constitution of Canada.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last night I was in process of outlining a series of steps which have been taken, and are still being taken, the result of which will be, if this resolution passes, that the parliament of Canada will have exclusive control over the Canadian constitution. Among those steps I had outlined the first three or four, starting with the statement of the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), made in the house in 1946, that, contrary to the generally accepted view of the constitution, the language rights guaranteed under section 133 of the British North America Act could in fact be changed by a simple majority vote of parliament. Carrying on from there, the next stage was the redistribution act, when the position was taken that the federal parliament has the absolute right to say what matters are or are not matters of provincial concern, and that because it was said the representation of a province in this house was a matter for the federal parliament, then however strong might be the views of the provinces in the matter, it was within the competence of this parliament to pass an act changing the basis of redistribution-contrary to the views formerly held with respect to the constitution.
Then there was the further position taken in the course of the debate on the admission of Newfoundland to confederation-the method followed there being a departure from the agreed terms outlined in the British North America Act-that a departure from the procedure set out in that act could be made by the federal parliament without any measure of consultation with or consent by the provinces as to the propriety or necessity of making that departure.
Then at this session we had the abolition of appeals to the privy council, the effect of which was, amongst other things, to deprive the provinces of what had been their right since confederation, their right of appeal to the privy council. That right was taken away from them without consultation or any attempt to obtain their consent. I think that is an important matter to bear in mind
British North America Act in view of the correspondence which has been received, and which was tabled yesterday, from some of the provincial premiers.
These were the steps which I had outlined when the house rose last night. I would like to outline three more steps which have been taken or are now being taken to complete the process of gathering into the hands of this parliament exclusive control over our constitution.
First, in the discussion of the question of the abolition of appeals to the privy council no heed was paid to the suggestion-indeed, the request-that when the supreme court was made the court of final jurisdiction some constitutional protection should be given the composition of that court, so that it might be made a part of our constitution, as it were, and that its composition might be changed only by means of a constitutional amendment. At the present time the Supreme Court of Canada is the exclusive creation of this parliament, and its composition can be changed by a simple act of parliament. As I shall have occasion to point out in a few moments, among the letters from provincial premiers in reference to the conference it is proposed to hold in the near future are several in which they request that the composition of the supreme court be taken into consideration before the final abolition of appeals to the privy council.
The next step I wish to mention is the one now before us in this resolution. I think it is important for us to have clearly in mind, in order to appreciate fully the consequences of the steps already taken and of this step, that if this proposal is adopted-and the government is putting the resolution forward for consideration and adoption-the dominion parliament is asserting in its final form the principle that it can amend the constitution without consultation with the provinces, and is taking that position in spite of the protests of five of the provinces which have expressed their views by letter. I should like to refer in detail to some of the letters which have been written. I think I should remark that if the Prime Minister had desired to prevent the public from being fully informed as to the views held by the various provincial governments, or if he had desired to prevent the full and informed discussion which should take place on this matter, he could not have served that purpose better than by the course he followed, in refraining from tabling this correspondence until yesterday, the very day this resolution came up for discussion in the house. That, I think, is remarkable, when one sees the lengths to which some of the provincial premiers have gone in the correspondence in expressing

British North America Act their views as to the propriety of this procedure, and in requesting that this resolution be withheld pending the convening of the conference it is proposed to hold following this session.
I have here a letter from the premier of Nova Scotia, dated September 27, three weeks before this resolution came up for discussion -and, incidentally, before the debate on the bill to abolish appeals to the privy council was concluded. The passage from Mr. Macdonald's letter which is of interest is as follows:
I observe that the Minister of Justice has introduced a bill for the abolition of appeals to the privy council. It seems to me that the abolition of appeals to the privy council might well form the subject of study by such a general conference as is envisaged in your letter. I beg to suggest, therefore, that final consideration of the bill now before the House of Commons be deferred until the conference suggested in your letter will be held. There is, I believe, considerable support for the view that the abolition of appeals to the privy council is in effect an amendment of the constitution and that, therefore, it is a question which should be the subject of discussion at the dominion-provincial conference which you suggest.
Two things emerge from that letter. The first is that the premier of Nova Scotia-and one or two other premiers held the same view-asked that the measure abolishing appeals to the privy council be deferred pending the conference. The second, and more important in the light of the present debate, is the view expressed in this letter that since it amounts to a constitutional amendment, it should be withheld pending that conference. Implicit in that view is the feeling that, before any positive steps are taken to amend our constitution, the provinces should be consulted, particularly before steps are taken to provide that the federal parliament, by its own simple majority, can amend our constitution without consultation with the provinces, in order that satisfactory assurances may be obtained that, in any such amendments, provincial rights will not be infringed upon.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: I have not a great deal of time left, but I will answer one question.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the privy council, the highest court of appeal, has already decided that this parliament can do away with appeals to the privy council?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: That matter is not in dispute.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Then how can it be a question of changing the constitution?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
That question was fully discussed in the course of the debate on the other bill, and if I were to refer to the details of that discussion probably I would be ruled

out of order. I may content myself with saying that the view that it would be in effect a change in the constitution likely to have an influence on provincial rights in the future was put forward in that debate. The premier of the hon. member's own province held the same view, and wished that the matter might be deferred until the whole question of the basis of constitutional amendments and related matters might be discussed at a dominion-provincial conference.
The letter from the premier of Quebec has been referred to already and has been published in full in the press; therefore I need not read extracts from it. However, he is another provincial premier who holds very strongly the view that before the question of constitutional amendment is decided there should be a conference with the provinces. The premier of Ontario also expressed his views as to the propriety of the procedure being followed, that is to say the propriety of deciding that the parliament of Canada can amend the constitution now and in future without previously discussing with the provinces the method to be followed, and at least trying to work out some safeguard which would allay the doubts and fears of the provinces that the method now being adopted may result in their constitutional rights being infringed upon. Under date of October 7 the premier of Ontario wrote as follows:
I am frankly in some doubt as to the advisability of dealing with the matter piecemeal without first attempting general agreement. Obviously, matters which are purely a federal concern will have to be delineated from time to time by the courts. My consideration of the matter leads me to believe that abolition of appeals to the privy council may affect this very important side of matters more than is generally realized.
The premier of Manitoba expressed himself in somewhat similar language. On October 6 Mr. Campbell wrote as follows:
Your letter indicates that your government has already decided to ask the United Kingdom parliament to amend the British North America Act so that the parliament of Canada would have authority to amend the constitution of Canada, but only in relation to matters not coming within the jurisdiction of the legislatures of the provinces nor affecting the rights and privileges with respect to education and to the use of the English and French languages. The government of Manitoba feels that there might be differences of opinion as to whether a proposed amendment to the constitution related only to federal matters or affected provincial interests, rights, or jurisdiction. Before agreeing to any specific proposal, therefore, our government will examine carefully the manner in which the provincial position is to be protected.
The letter from the premier of Saskatchewan, dated September 20, 1949, contains the following passage:
If such a step is taken, may I respectfully suggest that some measures should be adopted to make the Canadian supreme court more representative than

it is at present, in order that those who find it necessary to appeal decisions of the lower courts may feel more confident than they are at present that these matters are being approached from the broadest possible viewpoint.
Finally there is a letter from the premier of Alberta, from which lengthy extracts have already been quoted by the leader of the opposition, making it quite clear that the premier of Alberta holds the view that it is impossible for any one parliament to say what is a matter exclusively for its jurisdiction and what is a matter exclusively for the jurisdiction of other parliaments without giving some offence to the position and rights of those other parliaments. He therefore requests that this matter of working out a procedure of amending our constitution in Canada be left to be determined at the dominion-provincial conference which is to be called in the near future.
These are letters from five of the ten provinces, half the members of confederation, and representing well over half the population of Canada. They are written in terms which cast doubt upon the propriety of proceeding by unilateral action of this parliament to take into our own hands the power of amending the constitution in accordance with our views of what are federal rights and what may be provincial rights.
If only for the purpose, Mr. Speaker, of preserving unity; if only for the purpose of creating and preserving those conditions which would give some hope of success in trying to reach agreement at the dominion-provincial conference, I would have thought the government would have been willing for a few months to hold up the resolution now before us and to hold up these other matters which there will be five years to deal with, instead of completely overriding the expressed wishes of five provincial premiers and proceeding in the first month of this session with these important constitutional changes.
The final step to which I shall refer is again inherent in the resolution before us. It is the assertion, to which practical effect would be given by the passage of the resolution, that this parliament can decide what matters are federal and what matters are provincial. I know the Prime Minister said yesterday that no such thought is in his mind, that the decision on federal and provincial jurisdiction would be left to the courts. It is inherent in this resolution, Mr. Speaker, because it asks that power be given to this parliament to do what? To make amendments from time to time to the constitution of Canada, "except as regards matters coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures . . ." If these words mean anything, they can only mean that this parlia-
British North America Act ment will have to decide what matters are assigned exclusively to the legislatures. Having decided that, it will be said that all the rest of the matters are assigned to the federal parliament.
If we are qualified to make the first decision, we are certainly qualified and have to be qualified to make the second. If those words mean anything; if that definition of the power which it is sought to give to the federal parliament means anything, it means we are to be given that right and must exercise it. Then, having made our decision on what matters are federal, we are to be empowered to enact legislation concerning those matters by a simple majority vote of this parliament; that is the situation. We are being asked to do just that. This is the final step in a series of steps, culminating in the delivery of the constitution of Canada, tied and bound, to the sole and exclusive custody of this federal parliament. It is a position entirely unwarranted by and entirely inconsistent with the spirit in which confederation was achieved. It is inconsistent with any possible hope that some measure of general agreement may subsequently be achieved at the dominion-provincial conference, because the premiers of the provinces are being asked to attend a conference to talk about an amendment to the constitution, and at the same time are faced with a fait accompli. The federal government can then say: We have all the power we need to amend the constitution; it does not matter whether or not you agree here; we have that power and we are in a position to exercise it if we so desire. That is the position in which the provincial premiers will be when they come to the conference. Nothing could be better calculated to promote disunity and to ensure that disagreement will be the result of that conference.
Let us examine the position. I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not in his place, because I wanted to ask him if he would be kind enough, in the course of this debate, to say whether or not I am right in this proposition I am about to put forward.

The other day one of the other ministers had the same feeling, that he was a mind-reader. I am glad to find the Prime Minister numbers that amongst his accomplishments also, but perhaps since other hon. gentlemen may not be endowed with the gift of clairvoyance, the Prime Minister would be kind enough to make his answer later in the course of the debate, or the Minister of Justice might do it for him, so that we may all have the benefit of his great learning and his power to penetrate into the
884	HOUSE OF
British North America Act recesses of other people's minds. I would say he must be proceeding on that basis on this question of constitutional amendment.
The position is this. We now have it asserted that the federal parliament can amend the constitution without consultation with the provinces. The Supreme Court of Canada has been made the court of last resort in all cases arising in Canada. Parliament is now taking the right to amend our constitution in Canada. Based upon the result of those three steps, it will be only necessary for the federal government to insert in the preamble of any statute which it wishes to enact that whereas under section 91 of the British North America Act exclusive legislative power with regard to this matter was vested in the federal parliament, and whereas it is desirable to enact legislation dealing with the subject of the statute, therefore be it enacted, et cetera. By virtue of the declaration in the preamble that it is a matter assigned to the federal parliament, no matter what constitutional conflicts may have taken place previously with regard to the matter, the federal government takes power to legislate and thereby, in effect, amends the constitution with respect to provincial rights.
The hon. gentleman may say: But we have the Supreme Court of Canada; if any of the provinces object, let them appeal to the court. It is also a fact that the Supreme Court of Canada is the creation of the federal parliament. There is nothing in the constitution of that court to prevent the federal government from adding two, three, or half a dozen judges if it so desires. Let us suppose that a provincial government, in the course of a constitutional dispute, is faced with the necessity of submitting its case to the supreme court. It is faced with a court to which any number of judges may be added by the federal government, and the court itself will be faced with an act of the federal parliament declaring that "whereas legislative authority in this sphere has been assigned to the federal parliament under section 91, this parliament enacts as follows". The practical conclusion of the series of steps of which this is the final one is that the constitution becomes the property of this parliament of Canada, and the whole basis upon which confederation was previously founded has been altered by the unilateral act of this government and this parliament without so much as consultation with or the consent of any one of the parties to confederation.
The final point I want to make deals with the question whether or not the government has a mandate to enact this particular piece of legislation. Referring to this matter yesterday, the Prime Minister said that he and his government had a mandate to put


through this resolution. I put it forward unequivocably and definitely, Mr. Speaker, that in my view he has no mandate to put through the resolution which is now on the order paper and which will have the effect I have been describing, namely, of giving to the Canadian parliament the exclusive right to amend our constitution not only in particular but in general. If we look through the statements made by the right hon. gentleman during the course of the election campaign, we can find none to the effect that he was going to take that power. It is true that we find a number of statements to the effect that he would seek, in consultation with the provinces, to work out a method of amending at home the Canadian constitution. Yesterday when the right hon. gentleman read his own radio speech, he read the words in which he stated that proposition. I have just about finished, Mr. Speaker, but I want to emphasize this point. In his radio speech the right hon. gentleman said:
It is our intention, after the election, to consult the provincial governments with a view to working out a method, which will be satisfactory to all Canadians, of amending the constitution in Canada.
In my submission, sir, that is the only mandate that the right hon. gentleman received; but in the resolution that we are now being asked to pass he is exceeding his mandate in an entirely unwarranted and unjustifiable manner.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
As
this is the first time that I have risen to speak in this chamber since the opening of this session, Mr. Speaker, I want to take the opportunity of joining with the others who have already congratulated you upon your appointment to the high office you now occupy. We are all proud of the manner in which you are discharging the difficult duty of presiding over our deliberations.
In rising to participate in this debate, I feel that not many other opportunities will be given to us of discussing a problem of the importance of the one with which we are concerned in the present resolution. I think the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was right when, in the course of his speech delivered on the address, he referred to this first session of the twenty-first parliament as a constitutional session. Nobody will deny the fact that when the government of a country wishes to legislate in matters that directly or indirectly affect its constitution, it chooses then to legislate on matters of great importance not only to the present generation of its people but to future generations as well.
The resolution now under discussion will allow the realization of a constant wish of the Canadian people, and of what the hon. member

for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage), when he spoke on the address, described as a dream of his younger days. When constitutional measures have to receive our approval they must in the first place stand the test of time, and before we are called upon to consider them, they must also receive the sanction of the people.
In our democratic country no important measure of this kind should be dealt with by the elected representatives of the people before it has been submitted to the people of Canada and they have been given an opportunity of accepting it. Contrary to what has been said by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the leader of the government, when speaking on the subject in every province during the recent election campaign, clearly asked the people of Canada for a mandate on this question. Therefore the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had a clear mandate from the people before introducing the resolution which is now before the house. As a result of the decision of the leader of the government to get that mandate before introducing his resolution, we say today that it is with the consent of the overwhelming majority of the Canadian people, and with the approval of the overwhelming majority of the members of this house who are behind the leader of the government, that he is introducing this measure in the House of Commons.
I think that the Canadian public, which so well expressed its confidence in the Prime Minister and his party during the last election campaign, will be pleased with the attitude of our Prime Minister, who chooses to define, as he did in clear-cut statements, his attitude in public and national affairs instead of indulging in political manoeuvres. That is why we feel that it is with the complete support of the Canadian people that we are now trying to make this progress toward the complete independence of our country.
I approve, with joy and pride, the resolution which has been introduced; and I think I have the right today to say that I approved the spirit of it in the past, not only in this chamber but wherever an occasion was offered to me to express my views on constitutional matters. For example, in 1946, during the course of the debate on redistribution which has been referred to in the present debate, I had occasion in this house to give my opinion on some of our deficiencies with respect to our constitution. At that time, as reported on page 2248 of Hansard of 1946, I ventured to say:
Before concluding, I should like to say a few words with reference to the obligation resting upon us to have recourse to the imperial parliament in order to secure the remedy proposed by the terms of the resolution before us.
British North America Act
As I said before, it was a resolution on redistribution. I continue:
Every time the occasion arose we proudly proclaimed our complete independence within the commonwealth of British nations. We wish to believe, and we have a right to insist, since our country is now of adult age, that the Statute of Westminster be not a dead letter and was not adopted in vain. The most serious obstacle to the proclamation and the recognition of our sovereignty and of our complete autonomy lies in the fact that we do not yet possess our own constitution. Our constitution is embodied in an imperial statute; it does not even constitute a Canadian statute. That is why we must on every occasion undertake, perforce, that pilgrimage to London to ask others to decide upon our own destinies. So long as this anomaly has not disappeared from our national life, we shall not have the light to claim that Canada is a sovereign country.
It may be noted, Mr. Speaker, that my suggestion at the time was that we should have our own Canadian constitution embodied in our own legislation. In other words, I went so far as to claim that we should ask the imperial parliament to repeal the British North America Act so as to allow Canada to enact its own constitution as part of its own legislation and not part of the legislation of any other country, whatever may be the bonds and ties we have with that particular country. But I also think that Canada should not go too far and too fast in the conquest of its constitutional liberties if it does not wish to jeopardize by hasty measures its internal security as well as its relations with other countries, especially those with which we enjoy common economic and political interests.
The ultimate goal must not be endangered by measures of that kind, because the means that we would employ would not have been accompanied by the necessary precautions. Our constitution is indivisible. That has been said in this debate by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and it has been said before. I share the view of the leader of the opposition on that score, but I also think that when the Prime Minister expressed a desire to have a dominion-provincial conference to deal with these matters it was believed that that conference would give us the opportunity to make some progress in trying to give to our country complete independence one of these days by putting us in a position to have our own Canadian constitution. I think that is the meaning that one can take from the letter that was addressed by the Prime Minister to the premiers of the provinces.
Whether our constitution as it exists today is called a pact or whether it is called a statute, one thing is certain, namely, that we cannot cast aside the fact that there has to be, and there is actually, a division of powers

British North America Act between the original provinces and the central government. This division is clear with regard to certain powers that are plainly defined in the act, on which there can be no confusion. Section 91 defines the powers of the central government. In view of that clause in the British North America Act, which has been referred to as the residuary clause, we can say that the powers of the central government are exhaustive as they are set out in that act. On the other hand, the powers of the provinces are defined in section 92. This may look simple, but it is much more complicated than it appears on the surface. It is more complicated because there are powers which have been conferred not only on the central government but on the provincial governments as well. In different matters there is concurrent jurisdiction. For this reason it is difficult to define exactly what is the power vested in the central government and what is the power that belongs to the provincial legislatures. I do not know whether that was done voluntarily by those who consulted with each other to have the British North America Act enacted.
I say that it might have been voluntary, but we cannot be convinced of that, because if we read with care the Quebec resolutions, and the opinions that were expressed at the time, and if we try to analyse correctly the speeches that were made by the consulting authorities, we cannot come to the conclusion that this concurrent jurisdiction was then decided upon and agreed upon.
In the wording of the text, Mr. Speaker, there is conflict; but it must be borne in mind that the conflict is much more serious than that. It is much more serious because the act itself is not complete and could not be complete at the time. There were domains that could not have been explored at the time; and for this reason the British North America Act-although we cannot say that it is a mere draft-is silent on many subjects. In spite of the residuary clause to which I have made reference and which seems to favour the central power, with the advancing years bringing progress and development in Canada, new powers were created, and those powers were to be allocated either to the provincial legislatures or to the central government.
Who was to be the master and the judge in deciding upon these things? Who was to decide whether a certain power should be given to the provinces or to the central government? Who was to say, for instance, whether a power existed already and was already comprised in the definition of the act, or whether it was a totally new power or privilege? Who was to say that the power
[Mr. Pinard.f

was not only derivative, or, as it is called, ancillary to powers already existing by virtue of the sections to which I referred, namely, sections 91 and 92, as well as other sections of the British North America Act concerning the powers and privileges of the central government and of the provinces? I submit that is where the real confusion began.
In spite of the fact that the best jurists began to explore and experiment in that field of interpretation, there is today a good deal of confusion in the segregation of powers as between the provinces and the dominion. There were, and there still are today, many classes of opinion, and it is not enough to say that there are those who favour a greater centralization, and, on the other hand, those who are in favour, and only in favour, of provincial rights. There were other interests from outside of Canada-there were also interests inside of Canada-which, of course, brought about interpretations of the powers vested by the British North America Act either in the provinces or in the central government. As a result our courts and the privy council have had to hear a large number of cases, either concerned with private litigation or in the way of references from the central or provincial governments, in order to try to determine the boundary between the jurisdiction of the provinces and the central government. In spite of the fact that the judgments that have been rendered by those courts did not satisfy all interests, I think it can be said that a considerable job was done. The job was to try to establish the course to be followed by private interests as well as by the different governments in connection with matters affecting constitutional rights.
As the Prime Minister said last month when he answered the Leader of the Opposition, since the earliest days of confederation, judicial process has been one of the methods of deciding conflicts that have arisen from the division of powers as between the provinces and the central power. I submit that that is a normal procedure and undoubtedly it will continue. We shall still have to rely upon our courts to find out whether a certain matter is within the jurisdiction of the central government or of the provincial legislatures. That is the case not only in Canada but also in the neighbouring country to the south and in all other countries where there is a division of power between administrative groups.
For these reasons neither the provincial legislatures nor minority groups should have reason to fear that this legislation will endanger their rights or privileges. All one has to do is to read the resolution as drafted and one will conclude that both minority and

provincial rights are being protected. There is to be a clear distinction made between provincial and minority rights and those of the central government. Paragraph 1 of the resolution reads:
The amendment from time to time of the constitution of Canada, except as regards matters coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces-
Is that not a clear undertaking on the part of the government that in no case will there be an attempt made to amend the constitution in connection with matters that come within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments? The paragraph goes on to read:
-or as regards rights or privileges by this or any other constitutional act granted or secured to the legislature or the government of a province, or to any class of persons with respect to schools or as regards the use of the English or the French language.
In these words I find a clear decision on the part of the federal government not to interfere in matters affecting minority groups or the provincial governments. I submit that the purpose of this resolution is not to determine the boundary between provincial and dominion jurisdiction, nor is it intended to segregate the powers vested in the dominion or in the provinces; the purpose of the resolution is to make the central government master in its own house, as the provincial governments are now in theirs under the provisions of the British North America Act. The central government is simply asking for the same powers as have been conferred by the British North America Act on the legislatures of the provinces.
When a provincial government decides to change the number of representatives in the legislative assembly, by virtue of section 92 it does not have to have recourse either to the central government or to the imperial parliament. As has been done by the government of Ontario and the government of Quebec, this change is carried out of their own volition. But when the central government desires to increase the number of representatives in this chamber because of an increase in the population, we had to have the permission of the imperial parliament. It is to eliminate anomalies of this kind that the resolution is now before us.
I think a conference with the provinces would be most helpful in trying to determine the way in which to amend the constitution when we are concerned with matters affecting the provincial and dominion governments. I do not share the fear that has been expressed in certain quarters that the purpose of such a conference would be to determine what are the federal government's powers and what are the powers of the provincial governments. The purpose of the conference would
British North America Act be to study the question in order to clear up this matter which for many years has caused confusion in the minds of the people at large.
The adoption of this resolution will be a step toward the recognition by others and the confirmation by us of our complete autonomy and independence. For this reason I hope all provinces will be represented at the conference. We are informed that they have all indicated their intention to attend, although in the letter from the premier of Quebec I cannot find an indication of a formal decision by that government to do so. I hope that the government of Quebec will share in the common task, not only in words but in acts, in order to try to achieve for Canada a more complete autonomy. The premier of Quebec has often proclaimed himself as the defender of the provincial legislatures. I am not saying that he has no reason for thus proclaiming himself, although there have been times when we have had difficulty in trying to find the measure of his sincerity. But if the premier is the defender of the provincial legislatures, as he contends he is, I hope he will not become an enemy of the autonomy of Canada. I hope the premier of Quebec will not become an obstacle in this march forward by Canada toward complete autonomy and independence. Let us hope that this conference will bring about the result that we expect. By the adoption of this resolution we will have made a great advance toward complete independence for our country.
I want to conclude by reading a few sentences from an article which appeared under the pen of Mr. J. A. Hume in the issue of Saturday Night of the 23rd of August. The excerpt reads:
It will not be an easy task to work out these problems, but an adjustment of the constitution to changed conditions is necessary. No longer should Canada accept this strait-jacket which cramps her progress along the pathway toward adult nationhood.
I should also like to quote from the remarks of a former member of the house, made in a debate on a constitutional problem in 1935. He said:
Let us remember that the written constitution of Canada should be the servant and not the master of the people.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion now before the house. There is one deficiency in it to which attention has already been called during the course of the debate, and concerning which I shall offer an amendment. When I reach the point at which I wish to move that amendment I shall take a moment or two to express to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the hope that he
888	HOUSE OF
British North America Act will see fit to accept it in the spirit in which it is offered, and the hope that it may be passed by the house.
At the outset I should like to say a few words about the main argument advanced by the members of the Progressive Conservative and Social Credit groups against the passing of the resolution. Hon. members of the house who are opposed to the resolution have made it quite clear that they are not opposed to Canada having within her own borders the power to amend her own constitution. Their objection-and it has been stated quite clearly-is simply that they do not like to proceed with even a part of this important job without consulting the provinces. The only part of the task that is now before us relates to finding a way of amending the constitution with respect to matters that are exclusively federal. It is against doing that without consulting the provinces that the opponents of the measure have been speaking.
I take it it is recognized by all groups in the house that it is the part of wisdom and good statesmanship to consult the provinces, whether or not we are legally required to do so, so far as dominion-provincial or exclusively provincial matters are concerned. The opponents of the resolution want the principle of consultation to be applied, not only to finding a way of dealing with things that are dominion-provincial or exclusively provincial, but also to the finding of a way to amend the constitution with respect to things that are solely federal.
In the course of a debate that has taken as long as this, naturally a good many things have been said that some of us feel do not carry much weight; but I think it should be said in all fairness that a number of members, including the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), have stated fairly well the argument behind their point. I felt that perhaps the high point of the speech made by the leader of the opposition yesterday came when he talked in terms of doing our best to achieve and maintain all possible good will between the federal government and the various provincial governments. In my view that argument has to be considered and has to be met head on.
In reply to it I feel, despite the plausibility of the argument about consulting the provinces-before we take even the first step-so as to have their good will, that it would be a very dangerous precedent for us to adopt at the present time. Let me put it this way. We have amended our constitution a number of times since 1867, but there is something pivotal about this occasion. We are not just


amending the constitution in some one respect; we are amending the constitution with respect to the means of amending it. Whatever course is followed now will be a precedent that will be studied in years to come as we study today the things the fathers of confederation did prior to 1867.
Thus far the precedents are fairly clear. It is pretty hard to gainsay the argument advanced yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he pointed out that, out of eleven occasions on which the British North America Act had been amended thus far, in only three of those cases was consultation had with the provinces. In one case it was with only the four provinces that were affected, and in the other two cases it was with all of the then existing provinces. Therefore I suggest that if on this occasion we were to decide to consult the provinces we would be breaking the main trend of the precedents of the last eighty-two years, and we would be establishing a new precedent which, as I have already said, would be dangerous. Why do I say that? I say it because it really is quite clear what would happen if we consulted the provinces: it would convey the idea that we would be getting from them the right to amend the constitution as to federal matters. The very first time we sought to use that power the provinces would say: We gave you that power; consult us as to how you are going to use it.
I submit further that even the courts would have to pay same attention to the procedure followed in adopting the new class 1 of section 91. It seemed to me last night, when the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) was speaking, that he emphasized the first point I have just made. I think I am paraphrasing him faithfully when I say that he said he was prepared to go the whole way with his leader provided his leader would give him the assurance that there would not be any further amendments of the British North America Act without consulting the provinces. I feel that is exactly what would happen. If we were to consult the provinces about the first step we would have them saying afterwards: You got the right from us; consult us before you use that right to make any further changes in the British North America Act.
There is no doubt that in a country as large and as far-flung as Canada it is extremely important that certain rights and privileges in local areas should be recognized. I think it is that fact, rather than theory, that has led to the desirability of the federal structure. But surely the main aim of Canada should be to further the purpose of the fathers of confederation to fuse this far-flung land into

one great nation. I think it is highly important at this pivotal stage in our constitutional history that we make it clear that we are acting as a nation and not as a group of ten separate units. I believe it has been read before, possibly in the course of this debate, but I should like to put on the record again a paragraph from a speech made by the Hon. C. H. Cahan before the Canadian Club of Toronto, on September 15, 1937. As hon. members are aware, Mr. Cahan was secretary of state in the last Conservative government, and this is what he had to say:
As a young man I knew personally, and I might also say intimately, several of the leading statesmen then living, who had been engaged in promoting and drafting the British North America Act. I knew their views as publicly and privately expressed, and I am confident that, as founders of the Canadian confederation and framers of that act, they undoubtedly believed that they were establishing on the northern half of this continent a new Canadian nation. With that end in view, they sought to reserve to the national parliament such extensive legislative powers as would prove adequate to meet all national responsibilities which might thereafter, from time to time, arise, and thus avoid those deplorable conditions which had then so recently resulted in civil war in the neighbouring republic.
I point out to hon. gentlemen to my right that this excellent statement of the aims of the fathers of confederation, this fine statement of something which is in the hearts and minds of all Canadians, was made by the secretary of state of the Conservative government under the late Viscount Bennett. So it seems to me that when hon. members ask what is the urgency of the resolution now before us, the answer should be not that there is haste in the matter of time, this week rather than next week or next month, but rather that the priority should be clear, and that we should deal with matters which are exclusively federal before we hold the dominion-provincial conference, and we should thus make it clear that we do not need to go to the separate provinces as the source of a power which was given by the British North America Act to Canada as one great nation.
Then may I also call as a witness in this story another outstanding Conservative figure in this country, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. I am referring now to remarks he made when this matter of amending the constitution was under discussion in 1925. At that time a motion was before the house dealing with the desirability of Canada securing power to amend the constitution. I am reading this quotation from "Constitutional Issues in Canada, 1900-1931" by Robert MacGregor Dawson. The speeches of several members, delivered on February 18 and 19, 1925, are put together; and they appear in Hansard for
British North America Act that year at pages 297 to 300 and 335 to 337. Mr. Meighen's speech was one of those quoted, and I quote from it as follows:
In the first place, I do not think it would be a matter of convenience that the whole of the provinces of Canada should in every case consent. If we are going to put those obstacles in front of our course, we are going to add to the difficulties, if any did exist, that we have had in the past.
Now listen to these words by Mr. Meighen:
We have amended the British North America Act many times upon address of this house without speaking to the provinces at all. Why? Because the amendments we asked for did not affect in any way minority rights, did not affect in the remotest way provincial rights, were amendments in which the provinces or minorities were not concerned at all. It would be cumbersome indeed in such cases to be compelled to pass first from province to province and obtain universal approval.
I would submit that the words used by Mr. Meighen on that occasion apply exactly to what we are doing at the present time. The amendment we now seek does not affect in any way minority rights, does not affect in the remotest way provincial rights, and it is an amendment in which the provinces or minorities are not concerned at all. For that reason it seems to me we clearly have the right to pass this amendment; and, as I have been trying to indicate, I feel that we should do it in this way rather than make the mistake of reversing the trend of the last eighty-two years, which has been pretty clear, namely, that in federal matters the federal parliament has the authority and does not have to go to the provinces for consent to exercise that authority. Perhaps I have said it too often already, but I repeat that if now we went to them to ask for that authority we would be establishing a precedent that would bedevil constitutional matters for years to come.
In connection v/ith this whole matter I like very much the approach taken by Dr. Maurice Ollivier in his oft-quoted book, "Problems of Canadian Sovereignty". I refer particularly to the chapters headed "Statute or Contract" and "History of Amendments" and "Methods of Amendment," but I am going to quote specifically a few paragraphs. First I refer to pages 348 and 349, where Dr. Ollivier is dealing with the question whether the British North America Act is a contract or a statute, and also with the basic question whether the federal parliament has the right on its own to ask for amendments, without consulting the provinces. Here is what he says at page 348:
A confederation is a union of independent and sovereign states, bound together by a contract or treaty imposing the observance of certain conditions depending on the unanimous consent of the contracting parties who remain free to secede from the union. The states forming part of a confederation retain their political independence and are, from the point of view of internal ional law, recognized

British North America Act as sovereign states. The best example of such a confederation is the confederation of the Rhine created by Napoleon in 1805.
It is easy to see, then, why Canada is not a confederation. In effect the provinces have been fused or federated so as to form a juridical state enjoying all the privileges and rights appertaining to a sovereign and autonomous nation.
Then a little later, developing another argument, Dr. Ollivier quotes the late Norman Rogers, who at the time was a professor. I am now referring to pages 349 and 350:
It is evident that difficulties arise the moment we attempt to identify the parties to the alleged treaty or agreement of confederation. Is the dominion a party? It did not exist prior to the passing of the British North America Act. Are Ontario and Quebec parties to the agreement? They were not distinct provinces during the confederation negotiations, although it is true that Upper and Lower Canada were accorded a separate status at the Quebec and London conferences. Are Prince Edward Island and British Columbia parties to the contract? They made no agreement with the other provinces but only with the dominion. Are Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan to be regarded as parties to the agreement? They were created by acts of the dominion parliament.
"The crown did not authorize the delegates at the Quebec conference to conclude a binding agreement among themselves. All that was sanctioned by the dispatch to Lord Mulgrave was a conference on the subject of a union of the provinces of British North America."
Now I go to another quotation on pages 351 and 352, which arises from the argument Dr. Ollivier has been putting forward:
The preamble of the British North America Act furnishes proof that it does not proceed from a pact. It commences thus: "Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united," and not "considering that the provinces have concluded a treaty, a convention," or even "drawn up a project of convention with a view to federal union."
From these two propositions-
That is, the fact that the provinces are not sovereign states, as is the case in a confederation, and the fact that it is difficult to pick out the parties to the alleged pact.
-showing that we are not a confederation and that our constitution is not a contract, the third naturally follows, that, except in the very special cases which I will cite later-
That is, in matters having to do with provincial jurisdiction.
-the consent of all the provinces to an amendment to the constitution is not required.
The author goes on to quote many people on that phase of the matter, until finally he reaches the exciting part of his chapter beginning at page 359. At that point he is recounting the statements of witnesses who appeared before the special committee which dealt with this matter in 1935, and the witness being considered at the moment was Professor Kennedy of the university of Toronto.

I quote again from Dr. Ollivier's book at page 359:
Mr. Kennedy goes much further and says: "I do not think there is the slightest necessity in law for the parliament of Canada to consult the provinces in the process. It may be very good politics, but politics is not the law."
The committee had reached consideration of matters of provincial concern. The next paragraph in that book reads as follows:
It is unnecessary to add that this last declaration by the learned professor caused a sensation in the committee as may be realized from the discussion which immediately followed and which is here reproduced without change:
"Mr. Cowan:	Parliament could not do anything
with the powers which come under section 92.
"The Witness:	I think the parliament of Canada
can present any address to the parliament of the United Kingdom.
"Hon. Mr. Lapointe:	You would not advise this
parliament to do so.
"The Witness: I do not think it would be a very wise thing.
So, Dr. Ollivier develops the argument that there is no question but that the federal parliament has the right, on its own initiative, to request Westminster to amend the British North America Act with respect to any matter. It is made clear, however, that everyone recognizes it is the part of wisdom or the part of good politics, which means the part of good statesmanship, that when you come to matters that are of provincial concern you consult the provinces before such changes are made. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that should be our approach to the problem at this pivotal point in Canadian constitutional history. We should do what this resolution calls for, so far as clearly and exclusively federal matters are concerned, without consulting the provinces, so that we may avoid the pitfall of having the provinces say the federal government derives its powers to do so from the provinces. That position would bedevil us from this time forward. As wise statesmen, however, we should consult the provinces with regard to matters that are dominion-provincial or exclusively provincial before any change is made in the constitution in respect to matters of that kind.
In passing, I should like to answer one or two of the arguments that have been advanced. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said, as recorded at page 848 of Hansard, that no one was opposed to this country having the right to amend its own constitution, but he was opposed to unlimited power being reposed in this parliament. I am sure that when the hon. member reflects on the significance of this statement he will realize it was a bit far-fetched. The motion does not ask for unlimited power to be given to this parliament. The power is precisely limited by the terms of the motion that is

British North America Act
now before us. The member for Eglinton went on to say that the line of demarcation between matters that are federal and matters that are provincial is not clear. It seemed to me that the Prime Minister had already answered that argument. He said the terms of this new section were deliberately left without too specific a definition, so they would not interfere with the other lines that are already drawn in the British North America Act. This means that the courts will protect the federal and provincial parliaments from encroaching upon each other.
Yesterday the leader of the opposition said he did not like what we were doing because it did not provide a procedure. As a matter of fact, what we are doing is following the procedure that has been followed through the years. We are seeking an amendment of the British North America Act in the same way it has always been secured, by an address to His Majesty the King. This amendment deals exclusively with federal matters, and it is being sought in the manner in which amendments dealing with exclusively federal matters have always been attained, namely, through an address to His Majesty by the federal parliament without consulting the provinces. The leader of the opposition also said that, if this amendment were passed, the federal government might amend the constitution in such a way as to interfere with the taxing powers of the provinces. Section 91, subsection 3, says that the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation is within the federal power. This government, therefore, already has unlimited power in that field, so that the possibility of a future amendment making it wider is out of the question.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is another facet to this question about which we should be thinking, and that is the doublebarrelled interest Canadian people have in this question. There is no doubt in my mind that there is interest in it of a sentimental nature. I use that word "sentimental" in its best sense. Canadians do look forward to the day when, as a nation within the British commonwealth, we will nevertheless have all the marks of national sovereignty. On that sentimental basis, I do believe Canadians want us to get on with this job of bringing the control of our constitution to our own country.
But the people of Canada are interested in this question of amending the British North America Act for reasons other than sentiment. They are interested for substantial reasons as well. I believe all hon. members will agree with me that in recent years many requests for legislative changes, particularly
in the social security field, have been met with the reply that this or that cannot be done until the British North America Act has been amended. We are told that a proper contributory social security scheme cannot be put into effect until Canada can amend the British North America Act. It is because of these statements of a substantial nature that Canadians are keenly interested in securing amendment of the British North America Act. I want to say to the Prime Minister that unless the government speeds up a bit and does not act so much like the turtle to which the Liberal party has been compared in an interesting editorial in the current issue of Maclean's magazine, Canadians will not thank the Liberal party very much. Unless this government follows these constitutional amendments with an early use of the power to amend our own constitution to solve the social security problem, Canadians will not be grateful to the Liberal party for having taken these merely sentimental steps.
At times, when I have listened to the debate and heard the Liberals waxing eloquent about the steps that are being taken, and have heard the members of the Conservative party get all worked up about it, I have said to myself, "What are you quarrelling about?" The real issue is the next step. The real issue is the use of the power to amend the British North America Act so that this parliament will have the right to initiate over-all social security legislation as well as other things that the Canadian people want and have been promised time after time.
At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I indicated it was my intention to move an amendment. I shall do so in a moment or two, but before I do I should like to say that during the course of this debate my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), referred to the desirability and the necessity of entrenching the clause that has to do with the limiting of the life of a parliament. As a matter of fact, if the leader of the opposition had not moved an amendment which was so worded that no subamendment could be moved, my leader would have moved yesterday the amendment I am going to present to the house now. I believe everyone will agree-I am sure the Prime Minister will agree-that of equal importance with the necessity of entrenching minority rights, such as the use of the English and French languages, is the necessity of entrenching the right of all the people of Canada to be assured that a parliament will never run more than five years. Furthermore, the people should be assured that there will be a session every year.

British North America Act
At the moment, those two matters are guaranteed by specific sections in the British North America Act. For example, the section which deals with the matter to which I referred latterly, section 20, reads as follows:
There shall be a session of the parliament of Canada once at least in every year, so that twelve months shall not intervene between the last sitting of the parliament in one session and its first sitting in the next session.
Section 50 is the one that deals with the limitation upon the life of a parliament or, more specifically, upon the life of a House of Commons. Section 50 of the British North America Act reads as follows:
Every House of Commons shall continue for five years from the day of the return of the writs for choosing the house (subject to be sooner dissolved by the governor general), and no longer.
I submit, and urge as strongly as I can, that those two clauses should be entrenched beyond any possibility of amendment. I feel sure that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will agree that that should be done. They deal with the most sacred relationships between the government and parliament, and between parliament and the people. Those are matters that are exclusively federal. If they were left amendable by this parliament, they could be changed at any time by a majority vote; and to make such a change would be breaking faith with the people of the country. This is not just a theoretical or hypothetical question. As my leader pointed out yesterday, it has been done twice by provincial governments, exercising the same unlimited power that they have under their constitutions. The two examples were the provincial government of Ontario and the provincial government of Saskatchewan, both of which during the war years presented to their legislatures the necessary motion to extend the life of those legislatures. My leader reminds me that in both instances they were Liberal governments.
This matter can be taken care of easily by the insertion of a few words in the clause which is in the motion of the Prime Minister that is now before the house. The clause as he has worded it, and as I understand it, is fairly clear in what it seeks to do. It says- and with him I am in agreement one hundred per cent-that we should have the right to amend things that are exclusively federal but that we should entrench certain matters which obviously we should not have the right to amend. In the Prime Minister's wording of the resolution he has named two sets of things or, shall I say, three things that obviously we should not have the right to amend: powers assigned to the legislatures, matters relating to education, and matters relating to the use of the English and the French language. I submit that in the same

category as those things which obviously we should not have the power to amend goes this question of there having to be a session of parliament at least once each year and there having to be an election at least once in every five years. In fact, I regard these guarantees as two of democracy's most important bulwarks. Therefore I offer an amendment to take care of this matter, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). I move as follows:
That the resolution be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the word "language," in the fourth last line thereof, the following words:
"or as regards the requirement of section twenty of this act that there shall be a session of the parliament of Canada at least once each year, or as regards the requirement of section fifty of this act that no House of Commons shall continue for more than five years."

speechtext:
There again we have the argument which we have been through a good many times. You must rely at some point on the good sense, the wisdom and the good statesmanship of the people who are sent here. We now have the power, by a simple majority vote, to pass an address to His Majesty to make any change. But there are some things that we simply would not change. Part of my argument today was, by referring to Dr. Ollivier's book, to show how the authorities have dealt with this matter; they have taken the position that we have the power, but that there are some things which, though legal, it is not the part of wisdom or statesmanship to do, and which are simply not done. My contention is that putting this in the same category in which we put minority rights is the best legal protection we can give it; and by giving it that kind of protection and by making it as difficult to change as possible, we make it even more the part of wisdom and good statesmanship not to touch it.
Before I go further, just so that it will not be too far apart on the record, I should like to read the entire section as it would read with my amendment put into it. If my amendment carries, as I hope it will, the new section 1 of section 91 of the British North America Act will then read as follows:
1. The amendment from time to time of the constitution of Canada, except as regards matters coming within the classes of subjects by this act

assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces, or as regards rights or privileges by this or any other constitutional act granted or secured to the legislature or the government of a province, or to any class of persons with respect to schools or as regards the use of the English or the French language, or as regards the requirement of section twenty of this act that there shall be a session of the parliament of Canada at least once each year, or as regards the requirement of section fifty of this act that no House of Commons shall continue for more than five years.
I deeply appreciate the attention the Prime Minister has given to the whole of this debate, and particularly the attention he has given to my remarks this afternoon. I hope that he will consider this amendment favourably. If I may say so in public, one thing about the Prime Minister that has appealed to us is the fact that on several occasions he has shown himself to be big enough to accept suggestions that came from the opposite side of the house. That is good statesmanship and good politics too. We get enough of the other attitude, of course; that is, of suggestions being thrown out simply because they come from the other party. I am sure the Prime Minister feels as I have indicated about this matter. He knows how significant is this date in Canadian history. He realizes that this amendment touches an important point. I am sure he will agree with me that it ought to be entrenched as much as the other points in his motion, and I hope that he will agree to its being done.
If he would like to have this wording looked at by the law officers of the crown, and have the amendment slightly reworded in some respects so that it will meet any points the legal experts might raise, I should be glad to agree to any change in its wording. In other words, I am appealing to the Prime Minister to look upon this proposal in the spirit in which it is offered, and to agree with me that some way should be found in which this house can afford this desirable protection to two matters fundamental to our Canadian democracy.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to allow our country to amend its constitution without having to apply to a foreign parliament.
Unquestionably, this step has long been looked upon with favour by the country at large. It is hardly logical that a country like ours, whose part in world affairs is so important, should still have to go through a process so out of keeping with its status as a great democratic state.
It should be remembered, however, that the constitution of a country is the very basis of its nationhood; it is the document from which all statutes spring, not only those
British North America Act of the federal and provincial authorities but all laws applicable to the citizens of the country. In short, our constitution is the foundation of the Canadian nation. Therefore, parliament should be very cautious in bringing about any changes, especially as far as the allocation of amending powers to the various parties is concerned. In 1867, our country's population numbered only three and a half million inhabitants, of various races, creeds and cultures. If it has now developed into a strong and united country it is largely due to the foresight and political astuteness of the fathers of confederation.
It is only natural that a young country like ours, so rich in resources, should have developed beyond the expectations of these great statesmen. The time has now come to seek the power to amend the constitution ourselves, with a view to rendering it less rigid and more adequate.
All those who wish to see Canada take her proper place in the world as an autonomous and sovereign state are delighted to have this opportunity of providing the country with a new constitution, or rather of making it possible for Canada to amend her constitution with a view to rendering it more adequate and more practical.
The very fact, however, that we are a confederation makes it imperative that we should act with the utmost caution. To my mind, such caution is lacking in the procedure by which the government suggests to bring about this historic change.
As a matter of fact, a school of thought has always maintained, both here and abroad, that the British North America Act is a pact and not only a piece of legislation enacted by the parliament at Westminster. It is therefore contended that our constitution can be amended only after consultation with the contracting parties, that is to say with the various Canadian provinces.
The view that the B.N.A. Act is a compact or agreement between the provinces was expressed by the mover of the act in the House of Lords, Lord Carnarvon. He stated, in effect:
(Text):
The Quebec resolutions, with some slight changes, form the basis of a measure that I have now the honour to submit to parliament. To those resolutions all the British provinces in North America were, as I have said, consenting parties, and the measure founded upon them must be accepted as a treaty of union.
(Translation):
And Mr. Adderley, colonial secretary, stated in the House of Commons:
(Text):
If again, federation has in this case specially been a matter of most delicate treaty and compact be-

British North America Act
tween the provinces ... it is clearly necessary that there should be a third party ab extra to give sanction to the treaty made between them.
(Translation):
This opinion held by English statesmen at the time of confederation was reiterated not only by Conservative leaders in this country but even by the Liberal party's French-Cana-dian luminaries, the predecessors of the right hon. Prime Minister, such as the hon. Honors Mercier, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, the hon. P. J. A. Cardin and others.
The Hon. Honore Mercier stated:
There were provinces before there was a dominion and it is from them that the latter derived its powers. They are sovereign within the limits of their jurisdiction and any infringement upon this sovereignty is a violation of the federal pact.
In 1906, Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated the following:
Confederation is a compact made originally by four provinces, but adhered to by all the nine provinces who have entered it, and I submit to the judgment of this house and to the best consideration of its members, that this compact should not be lightly altered. It should be altered only for adequate cause, and after the provinces themselves have had an opportunity to pass judgment on the same.
And the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe stated in 1937:
The British North America Act is the result of long and difficult dealings and finally of a compromise to which the provinces have adhered through their official and qualified representatives. Therefore, it is a legal agreement in due form and freely ratified. It then follows that the "qualified authority" to bring changes to our national constitution are the provinces whose good will has made the alliance possible and whose unanimous good will is indispensable to any amendment which may be decided.
I am surprised that the Prime Minister should break that Liberal tradition and I am also astonished that the French-Canadian members who support the government should disown the theories expounded by their great leaders. However, even though the government does not admit the theory that a pact was made, I cannot understand why it is unwilling to consult the provinces before a resolution of such paramount importance is passed.
Besides, the Prime Minister knows that the people of his province desire such a consultation. He has admitted himself having made, during the last election campaign, the following promise:
It is our Intention, after the election, to consult the provincial governments with a view to working out a method, which will be satisfactory to all Canadians, of amending the constitution in Canada.
I do not know what caused him to change his mind in so short a time! It is claimed

that there is no point in consulting the provinces because the last dominion-provincial conferences came to naught. However, the government did call such a conference at the end of this session. It must be admitted that, under the circumstances, the government's position is not logical, to say the least.
The government claims that in taking this step it is not jeopardizing minority rights nor the educational provisions of the British North America Act.
Nevertheless, it again sets as a precedent that our constitution can be amended simply by a joint address of both houses to the imperial parliament without consultation with the provinces.
It is true that the resolution which is now before us contains a clause whereby the government indicates its intention to refrain from amending section 133 at this time. However, the government is setting a precedent, thus greatly endangering the rights of minorities.
As I said, the government is upholding a theory diametrically opposed to that expounded by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, the Hon. L. A. Tas-chereau, and all champions of traditional Liberalism in Quebec.
This theory is contrary to the very principles of confederation. I doubt very much indeed that the representatives of the province of Quebec would have agreed to confederation had they not obtained a formal guarantee that the provisions of section 133 would not be thrust aside in such a summary fashion. One of the greatest difficulties in interpreting the British North America Act lies in the very interpretation of the various responsibilities of federal and provincial governments. There is the stumbling block of the whole system. The act of 1867 defines of course certain powers as falling within the federal jurisdiction, and certain others within the provincial jurisdiction. But there are several taxation fields to which the provinces as well as the federal authority claim certain rights.
If, up to now, federal-provincial relations have been strained and have brought about so much controversy, it is because matters of joint concern were involved.
I doubt whether the government's way of proceeding in that connection will ever solve the problem. The central administration should not be the one to decide what matters come within its jurisdiction. The provincial authorities may have different opinions on the subject and it is only through consultation with them that we can examine the various opinions put forth and reach an agreement that will be in the interest of the country as

a whole. The government's action constitutes another step towards centralization which endangers national unity.
Canada is a confederation. Our people are satisfied with that mode of administration.
I sincerely believe it is the duty of the federal parliament to strengthen the constitution and not weaken it. I feel that, in acting as they do, with this resolution, the government are undermining the very foundations of confederation.
I therefore deem it my duty to vote against the motion.
