Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak for the first time in this house, you will allow me to congratulate you on your appointment to the office you now hold. From what I have seen in the past few weeks I am sure traditions of justice and fairness will continue to flourish in this house.
(Text):
I rise at this time because I feel it is my duty to state the reasons why I am going to vote for the resolution. I am going to vote for the resolution for three reasons which I shall try to explain to the house. According to the debate and discussion that have taken place so far it would appear that the feeling
British North America Act of hon. members is unanimous as far as the principle of the resolution is concerned. The main difference seems to be as to the procedure which has been suggested by this government to carry out the terms of the resolution.
I have listened to the speeches of hon. members of the opposition during this debate and have come to the conclusion that no concrete suggestions have been offered in connection with this resolution apart from the suggestion that there should be consultation with the provinces. Well, the government has consulted the provinces on this matter, and I would even go farther and say that they have consulted the people of the provinces. That was the main issue during the last election, and I know in my own riding it was the main issue.
The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) has stated that the premiers of the provinces should be consulted, but let me tell the hon. member that in my own riding the representative of the premier of Quebec, who claims to be the champion of minority rights, fought against me. Since I attended school,
I have followed the discussions that have taken place in connection with this and similar matters. I have here a book containing the proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference of 1945. It has been said over and over again that it is most important that the premiers should be consulted on this matter, but I should like to quote to the house an excerpt from this report of the proceedings of that dominion-provincial conference. I should like to refer to the reason given by the premier of Quebec for leaving or breaking up, if I may use my own words, that conference. I quote:
The Prime Minister of Quebec, for reasons already stated many times at this meeting-
At this point I ask the hon. member for Three Rivers to pay attention.
-owing to the pressure of business, has been obliged to leave for his office in Quebec City.
Is the constitution that important as to permit a premier to give up by sidetracking the issue?
The constitution is the thing which permits me to sit in the house, it is the thing that permitted me to be elected as the representative of my constituents, but that was considered to be not as important as certain provincial problems. I am not completely convinced of the sincerity of those words.
Let us go a step further and consider the question of minority rights. Right in the body of this resolution the minority groups are given a guarantee which they did not have before. We have heard many technical arguments put forth in an effort to convince
896	HOUSE OF
British North America Act us that the constitution should be looked upon as a treaty or pact between the provinces. That may be so. Other views have also been expressed that it might be a statute or a law. Let us assume that twenty-five or fifty years from now the Liberal party is not in power and somebody else comes along and takes the attitude that our constitution is a statute. In the body of the resolution there is a further guarantee of minority rights to that contained in the British North America Act. Feeling my responsibility as a member of this house, and having been elected by the people, I must say that the mandate I have received tells me to support the resolution within the scope of what it means.
I have a further important reason for voting for the resolution, which also has its origin in the people. I receive many letters every day from people asking me about certain projects and the power of the federal government or the provincial government to do certain things in different fields. In the house the other day there was a discussion about whether irrigation in Saskatchewan was a provincial or federal responsibility. After eighty-two years I believe that the people of Canada are most anxious that we should take an inventory and try to proceed along definite lines in order to further the progress of the country. One hears many discussions in public places which do not seem to have any end. The matter of the welfare of the people is discussed and whether the passing of legislation is handicapped in any way by the lack of clarity as to the jurisdiction of the federal and provincial governments. Day after day and year after year we keep looking into the past to find out who is going to enact welfare legislation, and the people of the country suffer in the meantime because of discussions that do not lead us anywhere.
I believe some members raised a question about the urgency displayed in bringing this matter to an end. The reason for doing so springs right from the needs of the people. On June 27 the people gave the government a green light to proceed. They expressed their confidence in the government and are prepared to leave the means to it provided minority rights are guaranteed. In the resolution, consideration has been given as far as minority rights are concerned, a distinction is made between provincial and federal matters, and matters which may not belong wholly to provincial or to federal jurisdiction. Therefore I am justified, by the mandate I received on the 27th of June, in voting for the resolution.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not think I would be called on until eight o'clock, but I wish to say something about the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) yesterday. The two old parties put me in mind of two old soldiers. They never die. The two old parties are being reconstructed and re-created in Canada today. Those who have gone before would not know them, if we are to believe what has been said in the past.
I wish to refer to a few matters which have come up in connection with the resolution. I have not had any opportunity to prepare. I had to attend the funeral in Toronto yesterday of a former mayor of that city, Mr. C. Alfred Maguire, and I did not arrive in Ottawa until midnight last night. Yesterday was the first day that I have been absent during this session, but he was my vice-chairman and I had to pay tribute to him and was glad to do so.
As to the resolution, I wish to say that I regret very much that the government has brought this question before the house and the country at the present time. As I said the other day, these matters are largely secondary. It is true that the resolution has been moved, and as far as the amendment is concerned I think it changes the resolution very little. The amendment only amends a minor part of the resolution, and the resolution and the amendment might be taken together so that members will not be speaking three or four times, lengthening the business of the house accordingly. In my view the amendment does not touch the matter at all. It simply provides for the submission to the house a little later on of some of the principles of the resolution. I regret very much that the house and the country have been troubled with amendments to the British North America Act at the present time.
As you know, the atomic bomb has been in the minds and hearts of the people of Canada a great deal lately. There are many other matters that are vastly more important than the resolution. You merely have to read together the resolution of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the other matters which have been proposed in the house and which were put before the country during the last election. For that reason I may say I am very much surprised at the electors of Canada. We are supposed to be the high court of parliament, and the resolution seems to ignore one of the cardinal principles of our constitution, namely, that the courts are subservient to the legislatures. That is one of the cardinal principles of the British constitution.

As much of the common law of England as was applicable to our circumstances was introduced into Canada by the Constitutional Act, 1791, at the time that act was passed. There are many matters which have been introduced into the debate on this measure. The other day the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) placed what I considered a totally irrelevant construction on the speeches which have been made so far regarding appeals to the privy council. He referred to the Canadian navy and all that kind of thing. He forgot that in 1938, before the second war, I pointed out in the house that on the Pacific, to which he was referring, we had an unprotected coast line from Puget sound to the southern Queen Charlotte islands, and had no defence there at all. He brought in the Canadian navy and the Canadian army and what they had done in the war, but I fail to see what that has to do with appeals to the privy council. It is far from it, and I think his reference was very much out of place.
I should like to say to him now that what has provided protection for our unprotected Pacific coast line from time immemorial, in the days of Louis XIV, Philip of Spain, the days of Napoleon, and twice in our generation, is the British fleet. Where would we have been in the Pacific but for the protection of the British fleet, and also in the Atlantic and everywhere else?
Coming to the resolution and the amendment, they must be taken together, though the amendment deals with only a very small part of the question. However, I am sure the house does not want two or three debates, but that we want to come to grips with this whole question. Is this the time for us to proceed in the method and manner indicated, or is it not? The hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) the other evening was referring to the method and manner of this procedure when he asked for amendments to this act. As my friend the premier of Quebec has said, there is no doubt at all that the contract was made. How did this resolution come about? It is founded on the Statute of Westminster, to which I was referring the other day and which has done nothing but disrupt the empire. It is a mischievous statute, which has wrecked our empire. It brought about the situation in India and in South Africa, and has divided our own country. I am a great admirer of the people of Quebec, and have been ever since I entered this house. When I was mayor of Toronto I received the commander of the French army, the Marshal of France, at the city hall, and paid tribute to the 65,000 soldiers from our city who had gone to France and Flanders 45781-57
British North America Act in the first war to aid the French people. I referred to the awful privations, the suffering, the trials and tribulations of the glorious French nation, which would live throughout history as an example of the most sublime patriotism.
My leader has taken a very fair stand in regard to this whole question. We had the Statute of Westminster. Then we had a royal commission appointed to consider amendments to the British North America Act, commonly known as the Rowell-Sirois commission. Its final report was very unfair to the two central provinces. If any changes are made in the British North America Act I am afraid it will be a bad thing. I am sorry that such matters as public health and education were not made matters of concurrent jurisdiction at the time of confederation, along with agriculture and other things. That was one of the mistakes made at that time. They do not have these provincial legislatures in Great Britain, where they have forty-seven million people. There they operate with local governments in charge of the municipalities, and it was a mistake in Canada to have two municipal systems, one within the other, created by section 92 of the British North America Act.
The members of this cabinet seem very much divided on this question. I regret that it has been brought forward at the present time because, as I say, it is only secondary. What is the reason for the rush to put this over now, in such a haphazard manner, without consulting the provinces, without consulting the bar association, and without giving anyone a chance to look into it? Apparently this house is supposed to adopt this resolution in the twinkling of an eye. I fail to see the reason for all the hurry. I believe the people should vote on it. Why should they not be given a chance to express an opinion on these changes? Many of the younger members have come up from the municipalities, where in many cases you cannot spend any money without a vote of the people. Here we are going to work and destroying the whole basis of confederation. It is by this resolution being made a political football, and you can call it nothing else. It is being kicked back and forth before the people of the provinces, and I believe the government was ill-advised in its attempt to rush this thing through in this way. As I have often said, the two old parties in this house are like old soldiers; they never die. In fact nowadays they are being re-created, with the hallelujah chorus; but the party opposite are forsaking the beliefs of their founders, and forgetting all about their former ideals, political and economic. Mr. Fielding and Sir
898	HOUSE OF
British North America Act Wilfrid Laurier would not approve of this. They were in favour of preferential trade in 1897 which, as I said the other day, has been hung on the sour apple tree like John Brown's body. My hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said that was a good place for it. Well, that would be a good place to hang some of the principles he has been espousing in the Montreal district. It seems to me the Liberal party has a different policy and platform for each city and province.	.
We on this side of the house have followed the same principles ever since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald. This resolution is founded upon provincialism and other things than strict legal principles. In my opinion it is political. Here is what Sir John A. Macdonald said in 1844, one hundred and five years ago:
I, therefore, need scarcely state my firm belief that the prosperity of Canada depends upon its permanent connections with the mother country-[DOT]
He was the founder of this party, and just before confederation formed the Liberal Conservative party. He went on to say:
-and that X shall resist to the utmost any attempt, from whatever quarter it may come, which may tend to weaken that union.
Forty-seven years afterwards, speaking in the same city in February, 1891, in his last campaign- he was again elected-Sir John re-affirmed the same doctrine of our close relationship with the mother country. He said:
"For a century and a half this country has grown and flourished under the protecting aegis of the British crown. Under the broad folds of the union jack, we enjoy the most ample liberty, we govern ourselves as we please, and at the same time we participate in the advantages which flow with association of the mightiest empire the world has ever seen. As for myself, my course is clear. A British subject I was born and a British subject I will die."
In the course of half a century, Sir John never failed to make the stand of Canada known, in its relation to the rest of the empire.
This resolution is founded upon status, sovereignty and autonomy. During the course of the debate we have heard the word *"colonialism". This new word has been introduced by the hon. Minister of Justice. Shortly, he will be the right honourable. Now, what is the answer to the hon. gentleman opposite? The answer is simply that a million men went overseas in the first war. They did not go over there under their own status to fight; nor were they worried about autonomy or sovereignty. They did not even consider whether they were being called "colonials". Those men went to fight for an ideal. One million went from the dominions and 130,000 of them fell on the field of battle. They are buried in Flanders. Sixty-five thousand from Toronto went to fight in France, and many are buried there. Those men went to fight for an ideal, the


greatest ideal free people ever had. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition was one of them. He was wounded. There were many good Liberals and good Conservatives among those men. Many men went from the province of Quebec and they were good soldiers. I know something about them and I saw the work they did.
Those men were all satisfied with the status of Canada, and its autonomy and sovereignty. They were not called "colonials" because they were not colonials. They were representing the dominions. The same thing happened in the second war, only the number of men was increased fivefold.
The cabinet seems to be divided on this question. There are some in favour of one policy and some in favour of another. One has to link many things together into this resolution to see why this thing has happened, and why it is being rushed in the House of Commons. This measure received very little consideration in the other place where a lot of this work seems to start. I believe the government is badly advised in moving this resolution forward, because it is only a secondary matter. One has to link up a lot of other things. There is a motion to be introduced between eight and nine o'clock tonight to replace the word "Dominion" by "Canada", and another concerning the office of the governor general. There are also motions concerning the flag and the national anthem. Those men who went overseas in the first and second wars thought the flag was good enough for them. The Union Jack covered the bodies of many of the soldiers from our city who were buried in Flanders and in France.
I wish to speak for only a few minutes about this matter. I am opposed to the whole policy of the government. As the Prime Minister said yesterday, it is true that the first ten or eleven amendments made to the British North America Act were largely federal amendments. They were technical descriptions of many kinds and were not opposed by the provinces. Do not forget, though, that we had to wait until the Statute of Westminster was passed-this empirewrecking statute, as I call it. I have with me a textbook, Wheare on the Statute of Westminster. This decision of the privy council was based on this statute. In my opinion, the privy council is not a court at all, but is a judicial committee of one of the houses of parliament of the United Kingdom. The only reason it meets in London is that that is the centre of the empire and is the place most convenient to the representatives of the dominions and the colonies.

London is the centre of the world. There is no reason why the privy council should not meet in the other dominions as well.
During the course of the last four parliaments I opposed and moved a six months hoist to private bills introduced by members of the C.C.F. which were related to this matter. There is a division of opinion on this matter amongst the members of the cabinet. The Postmaster General made a speech which is reported in the Montreal Star of September 20. I read this paper when I have an opportunity, but I have not had much chance to read even the Toronto papers recently. The Postmaster General was at a banquet and he attacked the premier of Quebec for his empty speeches.
The other day the premier of Quebec, Hon. Mr. Duplessis, made a speech in which he challenged the federal government on this matter. He was opening a bridge at St. Eustache and, in the course of his speech, he insisted on the province being consulted. The only way in which the parliament of the United Kingdom can be asked to pass a statute to amend the British North America Act is by an address of both houses of parliament. In this textbook to which I have referred, it is said that some of the provinces made a contract at the time of confederation. There is no doubt about that at all; there was a contract. There would be no confederation at all, there would be no British North America Act at all, had it not been for that contract which was broad enough to bring together the sectional interests of representatives who were four thousand miles apart. I say that when there is a division in the cabinet on this matter, the government should proceed cautiously.
At the opening of the bridge, the premier of Quebec and Mr. Sauve made speeches. The press report of that event reads as follows:
In his speech, Premier Duplessis recalled the memory of the St. Eustache patriots who, in 1837, fought to obtain responsible government, also events of 1841, when Quebec and Ontario were united, only to fail to come to reach accord on major national questions. In 1867, he said, representatives of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, had agreed on a confedera-tive pact, handing over to a central government powers to deal with national problems, but retaining unto themselves the full authority to deal with matters pertaining to the protection of their rights and privileges. It was a pact, a contract, not a statute as suggested by Prime Minister St. Laurent, a pact that could not be changed without the full consent of the parties concerned, signatories to the pact.
Now that is correct; there is no doubt about that. Here is the Liberal party in this twentieth century, and what are they going to do? They are going to prevent a British 45781-57i
British North America Act subject from making an appeal to the foot of the throne, or what we call making an appeal of grace.
My friend the Postmaster General made a speech the other day and I shall read the newspaper report of that speech:
The minister then attacked the speech made by Premier Maurice Duplessis of Quebec last Saturday at the Richelieu Club convention here. The premier had expressed fear that changes in the constitution as advocated by the Liberals at Ottawa, might reduce provincial autonomy and the rights and privileges of the French-Canadian people of Quebec.
"Mr. Duplessis is fond of grandiloquent speeches which may sound agreeable to the ear but are empty of meaning when examined by an impartial observer," said Mr. Rinfret. "He likes to talk about provincial autonomy and the right of the people of Quebec to govern themselves without interference from Ottawa centralizers. He often pretends that the racial and religious traditions of French Canadians are endangered by the Liberal policies as applied at Ottawa. This is really taking too much advantage of the good faith of the Quebec people.
Mr. Duplessis claims that nothing should be done by the Ottawa government to reduce the rights of the province to the full employment of its revenue derived from taxation," the minister continued.
That is right today too because in Ontario-objection has been raised to the division of the school taxes between the two schools-It will be remembered that a different system was illegally foisted on Saskatchewan and on the prairie provinces accordingly. The article continues:
"In fact, previous Quebec governments had to administer the province on a revenue of $50 million while the Duplessis administration finds means to collect $200 million in taxes. In addition, it obtains millions of dollars for education and social welfare from Ottawa" . . .
Mr. Rinfret said that articles 91 and 92 of the constitution delimit the respective taxation powers of the central government and the provinces. They also determine the over-all taxation powers of the dominion government whenever these powers are not specified. The constitution, too, makes it clear that Ottawa can impose direct taxes. Mr. Duplessis knows that perfectly well. But whenever he is faced with reality, his only answer and argument is "autonomy."
He belittles Duplessis. The article continues:
The minister scoffed at the Duplessis argument that the rights and privileges in respect of the Roman Catholic traditions and the French language in Quebec were endangered by the Ottawa plan-
And so they are, because as I say, the privy council had been the protector of minorities. They protected minorities by giving fair decisions. Do not forget that majorities have rights as well as minorities; and that is where he is wrong. The article continues:
"Mr. Duplessis seems to think," he remarked, "that the French Canadians elected by the people to represent them at Ottawa cease to be good French Canadians or sound religious men. This would be preposterous if it were not so clearly ridiculous. The Quebec representatives in the Senate and the House of Commons have no lessons to learn from Mr..
900	HOUSE OF
British North America Act
Duplessis in that respect. They are just as zealous for the preservation of the Catholic and French traditions of the French-speaking element of Canada as is the Quebec premier. A proof of that is their desire to see the rights of the French language e stended to all Canada,"

Mark those words, "all Canada".
-"instead of being restricted by article 133 of the constitution to Quebec and Ottawa. This will be done when the constitution is amended."
There were 878,000 French Canadians in the other provinces of Canada who would welcome additional rights for their native language. All other measures contained in the speech from the throne, Mr. Rinfret said, were designed to extend the national rights of all Canadians, thus furthering national unity so desirable for the welfare of the Canadian people.
In a parting shot at Premier Duplessis, Mr. Rinfret said that while the Liberal governments at Ottawa were adopting or extending social welfare benefits, the National Union government in this province was destroying the good effects of school legislation adopted when the Godbout government was in power, including free text books, and was thus imposing an additional burden on Quebec families. He suggested that the premier be less generous with empty speeches and more generous in his treatment of the Quebec people.
I have a few minutes more until six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to conclude my remarks before then. I do not believe in this way of doing business in the twentieth century because you have to include all these other subjects. There is one up for discussion at eight o'clock tonight. There are those other things to be read into the statute. They have to be read into this resolution. There is no doubt about that. I have read the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He reads it into the statute but he amends only a minor clause. You have got to take them together in order to understand it. I regret that this resolution has been brought forward at this time when we are faced with other more important questions, and when we as an empire stand at the parting of the ways. Look at what Russia is doing today. She knows all about the atomic bomb. She has it now. May I say to the hon. gentlemen who come from British Columbia that, at the instance of the United States, Russia was invited to come into the Pacific ten days before Japan fell. Mr. Churchill denied that he ever consented to it.
In the Pacific today we have no protection whatever. I was referring to it as our back door. Everybody knows that a burglar does not go to the front door. He goes to the back door. That is what I call the Pacific. We should have some protection. We have lost the protection of the British fleet. As I say, a burglar does not go to the front door. He usually goes to the back door and finds out whether the people are out, as hon. members know. As I say, I see no reason for bringing


these questions forward at the present time. It causes division in the country. It leads nowhere. We all know about being colonials. The biggest colonials I know of in the house are the Little Englanders, the little people who do not know where their protection came from for four centuries, in the days of Philip of Spain, Louis XIV, Napoleon, and twice in our generation. Where would we in Quebec and Ontario be but for that? The enemy were up the St. Lawrence. They came right up as far as Riviere du Loup. I saw the cove in which the submarine had been. A secret session of this house was held accordingly. Are these not more important matters than the one with which we are dealing? As a humble member of the House of Commons in all sincerity I ask: Is this what we call twentieth century Liberalism or not? If it is,
I think twentieth century Liberalism is going back one hundred years, because the resolution goes back that far. It destroys preferential trade for ever. I remember what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said the other day, and I made some remarks accordingly. It destroys all that, and that is what saved the dominion in the thirties. The Liberal party started it in 1897, through Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding. It was never finally carried out until the Ottawa agreements made a great success of it. Otherwise you would have had unemployment ten times worse than in the United States. For all the defence we get in this country we are depending on the United States today, if we are attacked on the Pacific or at any other place. We have been surrendering too much political, military, economic and financial responsibility. Now by this resolution we surrender judicial supremacy. To whom? To the people of the United States. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) said the other night, we are getting into this bill the principle of the judicial system of the United States. We have been warned of the great dangers that confront this country at the present time. I referred to this matter the other day, and to what we owe to nationalism, to the mother country, the flag, the anthem and all that kind of thing. These things have got to be read into the resolution. If you ask me, it is weakening and destroying the very basis on which this country joined confederation. I referred to the two old political parties being like two old soldiers; they never die. But they are changing the basis established by the founders of confederation. I referred to the principles of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Fielding and others. Is that Liberalism today? No. You have not the Liberalism of the past. The Liberalism of the past believed in these doctrines, political, economic and financial. They

believed in a real future for the country. You are going back on all those principles. True, it was not carried out in the thirties, but the authors of it were the gentlemen on the Liberal benches.
I do not doubt the sincerity of my hon. friends to the left. I do not question it at all. I have always been one of the hon. members who believed that anybody could have an opinion in this House of Commons. In 1923 I described the House of Commons as a large club where every hon. member could express his opinion freely, impartially and fairly as long as he had the floor. I have never denied the right to my opponents to have whatever opinions they wished for themselves. I do not think it could ever be charged against me that I showed a lack of ordinary Christian charity toward my political opponents. I have a great admiration for the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I have always had it. I knew him before he became a member of this house. At that time he was a leading member of the bar and one of the leading public men of Quebec. He used to visit our city as a member of the bar association. While I realize that, I believe that he is now raising secondary questions that could be left over, including all these that are wrapped up in it. He is causing a division in his own party on the subject from coast to coast. All these questions should be left for a better day until we know whether we are secure or not from the enemy which is now at the gates. He is going to be at the gates very shortly if he is not there already. We have to consider the questions in the manner which has been indicated. When hon. members look at the questions more fully they will find out that what I say is correct.
I should like to quote one or two paragraphs from what the Dean of Chichester said about the mind of man at the present time, because I believe there are greater issues than this for the government to deal with, namely, to be sure that we have security for all our citizens. This is what the dean said:
Why do wars happen? It is sometimes thought that it is the possession of armaments, or of large armaments, that is the ultimate cause of war. It used to be said that it was the armament makers- "the merchants of death"-who brought war about for their private profit. So people have proposed to eliminate war by reduction of armaments, or by complete disarmament. It is urged that all armaments-if armaments there be-should be under the control of the state and manufactured in state factories. But this is to confound symptoms with causes.
It is not armaments that make wars, but the people who have control of the armaments. Wars are not caused by things but by the mind of man. The United States, Great Britain, France, Holland,
British North America Act
Belgium, and Norway had greatly reduced their armaments after the first world war. Denmark had practically abolished armaments altogether. This did not save any of these countries. There was another country, populous and powerful, that was bending all its energies to the preparation for war, which was greatly encouraged in its preparations by the weakness of the peace-loving countries and their obvious unwillingness and unreadiness for war.
The truth is that wars in modern times are caused by the emergence of a group of determined men who are able to rouse and mobilize within their nation a passionate desire to expand and dominate. They aim at indoctrinating their people with a conviction of superiority, an imposing idea that they are destined to rule the world, because of their great strength and particularly because they alone possess the true political philosophy for which the whole of mankind is waiting. The kindling idea, universal in its scope, and simple in its expression, plus the sense of destiny, are essential to the war machine. Men and women need a great cause, or what appears to be a great cause, if they are to be keyed up to endure the vast sacrifices that war, and preparation for war, demands.
The dean gives this picture of Oak Ridge, Tennessee, where they are making the atomic bomb. He says they are making it a peaceful scene but it is the manufacturing plant which was the birthplace of the atomic bomb which is going to destroy the world. This is his concluding paragraph:
Fortunately the west can confront Russia with overwhelming strength in industry, munitions and manpower, and has established a lead in atomic research which will be immensely difficult for the Kremlin to overtake. It is our duty to do all in our power to preserve that lead.
Yet, assuming that a balance of power in our favour is maintained, the question remains, "Is this sufficient to enable the world to settle down? Is it conceivable that there can really be a secure and contented world while Russia holds half Europe in thrall? Can genuine peace be established while Europe is half slave and half free? Again, is not more than Europe involved? If Asia, besides China and including India, Burma and the East Indies, come under the Russian grip can there be world recovery?" These are questions for the second stage of the conflict in which we are all at present engaged. When retreat is forced on Russia somewhere, the scene may brighten everywhere.
The main point to remember about the atomic bomb is that its use may depend on the gradual restoration of a more civilized world. Humanity may have to face the question-which is the less unendurable, a vast physical destruction, or the surrender of the whole of mankind to a diabolical tyranny such as the world has never seen?
This shows the importance of other matters. Are we secure, or are we not? All these matters which we have been discussing today are purely secondary. This is a political bill. It is not an economic or a legal bill. For that reason I wish to protest against it. If this is Liberalism of the twentieth century I should like to know, because they are upsetting the basic doctrines of the founders of the Liberal party, which was a great party.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday evening we were debating a motion for the second reading of certain divorce bills. Many hon. members stated at that time that they were unfamiliar with the subject being discussed and therefore were not in position to pass an opinion. Feeling somewhat guilty in that respect I took the trouble on Saturday morning to go to the Senate clerk who was in charge of the petitions and the evidence in connection with these divorce bills and I saw the different petitions and the evidence that had been presented.
For the benefit of hon. members who are not familiar with the procedure perhaps I may be pardoned if I take a moment or two to outline it. First a petition must be made to the Senate by the person who feels himself or herself wronged. Then service is made upon the defendant or the respondent who may enter a defence if he so wishes. Then the case is called to be heard by the Senate and while the respondent has the right to appear, generally he does not. Counsel may be engaged by either side and a few members

of the Senate sit as a court to hear the evidence offered by the petitioner praying that he or she be granted a divorce.
After the Senate court has heard the evidence it is sent over to this house where it is examined by the appropriate clerk and hon. members may inspect the evidence if they wish. I may say that the evidence is much the same in all cases and is not very elevating to those who may wish to read it. Then a bill is presented here and we are asked to decide upon it.
During the course of my remarks on Friday evening I gave it as my opinion that we should not be trying to make divorce easier. As I said, there has been a tendency in all countries, especially since the first world war, in that direction. That tendency had been in evidence for a long time before that because of the materialistic trend of the age. But it has been growing ever since the first world war.
I remember over twenty-five years ago hearing the late G. K. Chesterton, the famous English writer, speak during a debate on divorce at the Oxford Union. This was some years before he joined the Catholic church but even at that time he held the Catholic view on marriage and divorce. At that time he said that if divorce went on as it was the university of Oxford would soon have to give new degrees or the degrees they were giving would not mean the same thing as they had in the past. He said that if things went on a B.A. would come to mean "bachelor again" and an M.A. would mean "married again".
The frequency of divorce in England has increased greatly during the last 25 years, and the full Christian view of the indissolubility and the sacramental nature of marriage is not held as firmly as it was before. I think hon. members who have taken part in this debate are on sound ground when they object to parliament hearing these divorce cases. It is simply carrying out the theory, with which I cannot agree, that this is the high court of parliament and that parliament can do anything except change a man into a woman or a woman into a man. If parliament cannot do that then it has been trying to do the next best thing. It has been trying to declare that a husband is no longer a husband and a wife is no longer a wife. Personally I would not want to support any bill granting a divorce because I believe that "what God has joined together, no man shall put asunder."
When the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) was speaking I think he indicated that he did not realize the technical nature of the subject he was dealing with. He said that in the province of Quebec there
Private Bills-Divorce
was a way of dissolving a marriage; that it was not called a divorce but rather an annulment. He said that in any event there was a separation and the result was the same. I think I know what my hon. friend was trying to say.
Since no hon. member from Quebec rose to contradict him I feel that his statement should be contradicted for the purposes of the record. The teaching of the Catholic church in Quebec is the same as the teaching of the Catholic church in any country. When the hon. member said that in Quebec there was a way of dissolving a marriage, he was completely wrong. There is no way of dissolving a marriage. Once a marriage, always a marriage. He said that it was not called a divorce, but an annulment. Here it is necessary to make a careful distinction. The word "divorce" in popular parlance means to separate permanently; it is derived from the Latin word "divortium" which means to separate. However, in the English language it now is understood to mean a dissolution of marriage.
Annulment presupposes that there has been no marriage. All that the ecclesiastical court decides is that there never was a marriage. Many causes may exist to warrant the declaration that there has never been a marriage. As in the case of ordinary contracts, the court may say that there has never been a contract. I shall not enumerate all the causes that might induce an ecclesiastical court to say that there has never been a marriage, but I might cite an extreme case. If a man married his grandmother it could be held that that was not a marriage because it would have been forbidden in the first place.
"In any event", the hon. member said, "there had been a separation and the result was the same." There are several errors in that one sentence. The hon. member said that there was a separation. If he meant to say that in divorce there is a separation, he did not say enough. What we understand by divorce is a complete dissolution where the parties are allowed by parliament, or by the civil courts in the provinces other than Quebec and Newfoundland, to go their own way and to go through another form of marriage if they wish.
If the hon. member meant that by annulment there is a separation and the result is the same as in divorce, then he was completely wrong. A separation permits the parties to come together again when the bad feelings that may have existed between them have subsided. They may again take up their matrimonial duties and live as man and wife. In annulment according to Catholic teaching, the parties are perfectly free to marry, but in divorce, they may not marry

Private Bills-Divorce
again. It will be seen that this subject has many technical difficulties, and, as hon. members have indicated, it is probably the most unsuitable subject for parliament to deal with. Most hon. members have not the time or inclination to study the facts, and I feel sure there are many members who do not feel any disposition to deal with this subject at all. I felt that I should make these observations. As far as I am concerned I propose to vote against the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to prolong this debate. The other evening certain statements were made regarding the right of parliament to grant divorces. Like all Canadians I am against income tax, like most Canadians I am against sin and like most Roman Catholics I am against divorce. In the province of Nova Scotia we have a divorce law which we took over from England, together with other laws, at the time that the English, the Scots and the Irish came to our province. We had to adopt all the common law and statute law that was good for the circumstances of our province at that time. Among the laws that we took over was the divorce law. For years in the province of Nova Scotia there was one judge assigned to hearing divorce cases, and he could hear divorce cases only in the city of Halifax. It became more or less of a farce for those who had to inhabit the courthouse, which is the place where the judges of the court of appeal and the judges of the supreme court reside.
A few years ago a couple of us went to the government of Nova Scotia and then to certain of the law officers of Canada. We asked for a change in the method of hearing divorces. Today we have in the province of Nova Scotia a law enacted three years ago, I believe, whereby divorces are tried on circuit, and every judge must hear and determine divorce cases if they come before him. It was said at the time that greater opportunities would be afforded to those who wanted to procure divorces if they could get them in their own circuits. I took the ground at that time-and the bases of the ground have been fulfilled so far as I am concerned -that when people who were getting divorces on certain grounds came to the court at Halifax very few spectators were allowed and the people from their immediate neighbourhoods would not know that they were such scoundrels. I refer to collusion and that kind of thing.
The result is that today in the province of Nova Scotia there are less divorces proportionately than there were previously, and they are also published today. I had to try

divorce cases. I took it as a responsibility. I think that the parliament of Canada is a judiciary so far as the hearing of divorces is concerned. Every person who sits in the house and votes on a divorce bill is acting as a judge. He is acting as a judge because he is giving a decision on a purely legal matter but he is giving a decision on evidence that is not heard before this house. It is the same situation when a judge hears a case, and after hearing certain evidence finds that it is necessary to send out a commission to take the evidence of persons who are unable to come to court, who may be in foreign countries, or something of that kind.
It is true that one cannot say that a witness whose evidence is heard on commission is either a liar or a truthful man, but a judge can make certain inferences. That is the position members of the House of Commons are in at the present time. The evidence is heard in the Senate. I understand it is heard and adjudged by lawyers who know the value of evidence and the causes for divorce. I suppose it is all right to use the word "Senate" in this case, Mr. Speaker, because this is a different question. We are really discussing a bill that comes from the Senate. I know the rule about using the expression, "the other place", but in discussing this particular bill hon. members might have some idea that I was referring to something else if I said "the other place".
That is the situation as I understand it. I spoke a moment ago about taking over the law on divorce from England in the province of Nova Scotia, and I presume Ontario was in the same category.
Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
There are well established laws regarding the causes for divorce. In our province there are two, adultery and mental or physical cruelty. I think perhaps the same is true here.
No cruelty.

No cruelty. I know, however, what the law is in that regard in the province of Nova Scotia. The great difficulty in the present set-up, in the way of parliament granting divorces, is that, as I believe, the Senate often does not make sufficient investigation of these cases so far as collusion is concerned. I sat in the house from 1911 to 1921. I took a keen interest in the matter of divorce, and as a matter of fact in all private bills. On two occasions I was instrumental, along with others who supported my argument, in refusing to assent to divorce bills that came from the Senate. In one case there was not sufficient evidence, and in the

other there was clear evidence of collusion. Because they were acting as representatives of the people and as judges in passing these laws, hon. members should take the time, and sufficient interest, in these bills to see that no bill passes the house unless there is ample evidence to lay a foundation for divorce.
I am making this statement because of certain things that were said the other night on these bills, and perhaps certain things that have been said tonight. I am a firm adherent to the laws on marriage of the Roman Catholic church so far as they have been promulgated generally up to the present time, and I hope for all time to come, but I do not think that justifies me in voting against a divorce bill when it comes to this house because I am a Roman Catholic or because I adhere strictly to the laws of that church on the question of divorce.
We are all against murder; we are all against all kinds of immorality, if you want to put it that way. But if the house should take the attitude that we are not supposed to legislate on murder or any other kind of immorality, then we would be placing ourselves in a most precarious position as legislators and as judges. I have looked at the evidence in most of these cases. Even if I had not, I know how these matters are carried on in the other place, the other good place. I have been following divorces in parliament over the years, not only during the time 1 was here. I have closely followed the procedure by which this parliament deals with divorces and passes these bills, and I feel quite sure that it is a rare thing for any bill to come to this house from the other place without an abundance of evidence, which would be amply sufficient for these people to get divorces if they went to the courts of the country.
I am making this explanation, Mr. Speaker, because there may be people in this house, as there are people outside it, who think that because a man follows the doctrine of marriage as promulgated through the ages by the Roman Catholic church he is in conscience bound to vote against divorces. As hon. members know, I occupied a position on the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and I did not think I would be fulfilling the obligations of my oath if I did not decide divorce cases; for one of the reasons I was appointed was to take the responsibility for deciding any case that might be brought before me, divorce or otherwise. And I consider myself in exactly the same position tonight as when I held a responsible position in the judiciary of Nova Scotia.
The suggestion has been advanced that the province of Quebec should establish its own <*5781-58

divorce courts. That is a matter for the legislature of Quebec. No person within or without this house has the right to say that Quebec should establish its own divorce courts.
We do not want divorce courts in Quebec.

I know that, but suggestions have been advanced in this house ever since it has had to deal with divorces that as a matter of faith Quebec should establish its own divorce courts. I say that is their business, not ours. I remember reading some time ago that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), when Minister of Justice, went exhaustively into the matter of divorce in the province of Quebec, in an endeavour to find some method of removing divorces from the parliament of Canada. That seems very difficult to do. Personally I should like to see divorce divorced from this parliament, but the question is how to deal with people in Quebec who want divorces to which under our laws they are entitled.
I am sorry to have taken up so much time, Mr. Speaker. It was more as a personal matter, in order to explain my position, that I rose this evening.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has covered a great deal of the ground I intended to cover, and I compliment him upon the honesty of his remarks to this house. However, in view of the statements that have been made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), I feel that a number of new members of this house may not be as familiar as they should be with these petitions to the Senate, and I propose to cover that matter briefly.
I regret that the hon. member for Nanaimo is not in his seat, though I presume he will be here later. In his remarks on this subject the hon. member said, at page 799 of Hansard:
I feel humiliated that I should have sat here during the whole of the last parliament of Canada and on various occasions have seen twenty, thirty, forty or fifty bills asking for the relief of various individuals presented before this House of Commons. I wondered why these bills were presented to the House of Commons. I did not have the wisdom nor the courage to stand up on my feet and to ask why it is necessary that this type of bill should be passed through the House of Commons without any questions being asked. . . .
I may be to blame. It may be that I should have examined more carefully the bills which had been passed in the other place.
The hon. member is a man of mature age, and admits having sat in this house for four years before this session. He had a galaxy of brilliant lawyers sitting on his side of the house, including our friend whom I may call "Buttercup", who would have been quite prepared to advise the hon. member on the

Private Bills-Divorce
law of divorce. In the army we would have called that very poor staff work, to say the least. In any event it seems to me the procedure here is quite clear. Any member of this house may attend when these bills are going through the Senate. As a matter of fact I understand that a member of the Conservative party in the Senate is in charge of that committee. The evidence is given under oath. The remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo disturbed some of the younger members from Saskatchewan who are not familiar with the practice in this house. Not only may they go there, but I understand that members of the Senate will permit them to ask any question they wish, or to put such questions through a member of the committee. Some of the members of that Senate committee are skilled lawyers, who cross-examine the witnesses. They are put through the same type of crossexamination they would probably face in court. In addition to that, when these bills come to this house they are sent to the committee on private bills, together with a copy of the evidence taken under oath. In that committee hon. members have the right to re-cross-examine the witnesses if they wish, or to question any bill relating to divorce that may come before this house. So the fault lies with the hon. member for Nanaimo if he was disturbed and perturbed as a result of not being familiar with the procedure of this house, or following the facetious remarks of the hon. member for Yorkton.
As far as the law of divorce is concerned, we in the west always proceeded by petition until certain cases were decided by the courts of appeal of Alberta and Manitoba. Those cases were Board v. Board and Walker v. Walker, the citations for which I have before me, in which it was found that the provincial courts had jurisdiction in divorce matters. In Ontario, which perhaps sets a precedent for this house, they passed a divorce act in 1930 which was passed in turn by the federal government, under which the law of England concerning the dissolution and annulment of marriage, as that law existed on the 15th day of July, 1870, in so far as it could be made to apply in the province of Ontario was declared to be in force in that province. In Nova Scotia the law of divorce is different from that of the western provinces or Ontario. In Nova Scotia, under a statute of that province, a divorce may be obtained not only on the ground of adultery but on the ground of cruelty. So the laws concerning divorce are not uniform in our provinces.
Some question was raised about Newfoundland. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) has spoken twice on this matter but has not yet given us the law of Newfoundland with respect to divorce. Up

to the time Newfoundland joined confederation, they had no law of divorce. In the consolidated statutes of Newfoundland, page 53, section 17, there is the following:
Our said governor is not to assent in our name to any bill of any of the classes hereinafter specified, that is to say:
1. Any bill for divorce of persons joined together in holy matrimony.
In the white book that has been filed in this house relating to Newfoundland, being the report and documents relating to the negotiations for the union of Newfoundland with Canada, the memorandum of agreement entered into on December 11, 1948, between Canada and Newfoundland, contains in clause 7 the following:
The constitution of Newfoundland as it existed immediately prior to the sixteenth day of February, 1934, is revived at the date of union and shall, subject to these terms and the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1946, continue as the constitution of the province of Newfoundland from and after the date of union, until altered under the authority of the said acts.
Clause 9 of that memorandum reads as follows:
The constitution of the executive authority of Newfoundland as it existed immediately prior to the sixteenth day of February, 1934, shall, subject to these terms and the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1946, continue as the constitution of the executive authority of the province of Newfoundland from and after the date of union, until altered under the authority of the said acts.
Clause 18, subsection 1, contains a further provision bringing in the British North America Act. I believe the whole effect of the statute of Newfoundland is that the people of Newfoundland can now do the same as the people of the province of Quebec, namely, petition the Senate for a divorce. As a matter of fact, one petition has already been received and filed. The required sixty days will expire on the 13th of November. It is a petition for divorce from the province of Newfoundland, but out of deference to the petitioning parties I shall not do as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) did, and mention the names of the petitioners.
In so far as the whole matter is concerned, I am not going to enter into a discussion of the pros and cons of divorce. Those of us who practise law, and there are many in this house, know something about this matter. I agree with many of the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I seldom agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and did not wholly agree with the statements he made about divorce. After all, people are human. I believe the average practising lawyer who has handled divorce cases found that, during the last war when the boys were overseas for five years and away from their families, roughly seventy per cent of the

divorces that went through the legal offices of the dominion were in connection with service people. It was an unfortunate circumstance, but it was there.
Many of us know of families whose lives have been unbearable because the parents cannot agree. The effect on the children has to be considered when the parents are disputing all the time or carrying on in an immoral manner with other people. That is not conducive to a happy family life. I agree with the previous speaker, who served as a judge. When I hear members say in this house that they cannot vote for a divorce bill, I wonder about the position of the judges of our high courts in those provinces of the dominion in which divorces are granted. Many of those judges are Roman Catholics, and some are Anglicans. I have talked with them and I know they do not feel any happier than the hon. members here about granting divorces. In view of the law of this land as it existed when the British North America Act was put into effect, however, they feel that they have to carry out their duty as citizens of this country. All of us, whether we are Protestants or Roman Catholics, have the greatest respect for the religion of the other party. I do not think there is any member from Saskatchewan on the Liberal side of this house who is going to suggest that the province of Quebec or the province of Newfoundland should establish their own divorce courts. That is a matter for the people of those provinces to decide in the future.
In this country, the only machinery provided for the people of those provinces to obtain a divorce is the machinery provided in the act of union, namely, the British North America Act, which gives to the parliament of Canada sole jurisdiction in the matter of matrimonial causes. It is our duty as members of this house to carry out the provisions of that section. In view of those circumstances, I believe more or less a tempest in a teapot has been raised for the poor chairman of that committee. I understand this matter has been raised continually in this house, but the divorces have been granted, regardless of what party was in power. This is the only procedure by which those parties can get a divorce. We do not want a political football made out of a matter of divorce or religion, so I do not believe any government is going to take it upon its shoulders to change these provisions. If the private members of this house are sincere they may arrive at some different method. Personally, I do not know what that method is and I do not attempt to suggest it.
In view of the discussion that has taken place and in view of the fact there are a
Private Bills-Divorce
number of new members in this house whom the remarks of the member for Nanaimo might have upset, I thought it was my duty to make this explanation.

Mr. Speaker, having listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll), I noted that he was careful to underline the fact that he was speaking as a private member. I am speaking also as a private member. This is not a matter for politics. In view of the exalted position which the hon. member, before he entered this house, held as a member of the judiciary of the province of Nova Scotia, in view of the position he holds as a member of this house, and in view of the fact he has declared he is a Roman Catholic, but is nevertheless going to vote in favour of these divorce bills, I think it is my duty also as a Roman Catholic and a member from the province of Quebec, which is opposed to divorce, to make this statement. I am opposed to divorce, not only because my religion is opposed to it, but because it is the scourge of our modern society. I believe the less divorce we have the better.
I should like to point out to the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, who has preceded me in this debate, that he said that in voting on these bills he was acting in the same capacity as he acted when he was a judge in the province of Nova Scotia. I would beg leave, Mr. Speaker, to point out there is a great difference between the judicial and the legal process. Acting as a judge, the hon. member had to apply the laws as they were. When he took his oath of office he pledged himself to apply those laws. As a legislator, he does not have to pass laws to which he is opposed in his conscience. I should like to underline that point.
I should like to take issue with the comparison the member made when he talked about murder. It was his idea that if we decided in this house not to legislate about murder, because we are opposed to murder, we would find ourselves in a very difficult situation. May I point out that when we legislate concerning murder we legislate against murder in order to repress it or punish those who commit murder. When we legislate in favour of divorce bills, or when we vote in favour of divorce bills, we are not voting against divorce but are aiding and abetting divorce. For those reasons, I shall vote against these bills.

Mr. Speaker, I was a member of the committee on private bills for a great many years. This system of granting divorces was considered then and is all wrong. I may say that, in my opinion,

Private Bills-Divorce
the state should look after the wives and children who are affected by desertion. Divorce follows every great war. Away back in 1801, the same problem was faced by the Addington administration. So did the two Pitts. They had to face the same thing. It is one of the consequences of war. In the church to which I belong, as a humble member-and that is the Church of England-the belief is this: those whom God has joined together, let no man put asunder. That was the principle of the conference in England for a great many years. Recently a committee appointed by the houses of parliament has been considering this whole problem. It is presided over by the Right Hon. and Right Rev. William Charles Wand, Bishop of London, who succeeded Bishop Winnington-Ingram. Over there, because of the way the country has been devastated by war, and for other reasons, the desire seems to be to extend the principle of divorce to include a great many things that were not considered before as grounds for it; one of these is desertion, and there are seven or eight other matters connected with it. I was glad to hear some of the members here tonight speak on this matter, including the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, who has just recently entered this house again. He is a learned man, formerly the Hon. Mr. Justice Carroll. I welcome the hon. member and congratulate him on his address tonight. He was formerly a member of the house and did a great deal of valuable work in connection with the national fuel supply. May I also congratulate the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart), who is a bencher of the law society from Regina. It is a wonder to me that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is not one of the benchers because I look upon him as one of the best lawyers in the prairies.
Let me say this one thing further. In my humble opinion the state should do something to look after the wives and the children. Every state has people of this type. After every war it has these people and they are a direct charge on the municipality. I know that because I was head of a municipality. I know that they become a charge on the municipality not only for school purposes but for housing and many other matters like that. I believe that the time is coming when we should have some other system adopted by parliament for this work. When I was on that committee I noticed that we knew nothing about the bills. There is a principle of Roman law to the effect that marriage is a contract. The common law of England has been largely copied from Roman law. That has been the principle which has been

adopted in this country also. It seems to me that we should provide a better system accordingly.
In connection with this matter I want to point out that there is in existence a registration system. While I admit that it cannot be so in the province of Quebec, there is a registration system operated by the provinces. For what? For deaths and marriages. They have a register with the town or village clerk to that effect. In a great many of the provinces that law regarding these matters might prevail also; but in Quebec I admit that there is a different principle involved. No one wants to change their law. Far from it. I would never try to change their law because I believe that the majority of the people are entitled to have their say themselves.
In conclusion, may I say that I think we should have a conference of the two houses of parliament, because it has been largely the prerogative of the Senate to hear and examine witnesses and all that sort of thing. I do not believe in the system. In the United States, after many wars, divorce is becoming a canker in almost every state. As I say, it follows largely as a result of wars. There is a registration system for deaths and marriages in existence in some of the provinces. I do not see why that system cannot be adopted. No doubt a different system would be required in the great province of Quebec. The archbishop who was investigating this question is travelling in the United States at the present time. He succeeded Bishop Winnington-Ingram, the great bishop of London, England. He is visiting the United States at the present moment and is going into all these questions. He recognizes that the divorce laws should be extended to include desertion, and I think there are five or six other matters connected with it, where the children and wives are left as a charge on the state.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 14, respecting the revised statutes of Canada.
He said: This bill, Mr. Speaker, is to amend subsection 1 of section 5 of the act respecting the revised statutes of Canada which was adopted during the session of 1947-48. The amendment provides for the addition of the following words:
-and whenever in the said statutes or acts, or amendments thereto, the expression "Dominion of Canada" is used, there shall be substituted therefor the expression "Canada," or "Canadian" or "federal," respectively, or such other adequate word as the context requires.
The reason for this amendment is to be found in the fact that, since Canada has ceased to be a dominion and has become a
Revised Statutes of Canada Act sovereign state, the word "dominion" as applied to Canada has entirely lost its original meaning. The word "dominion" is a very old one, Mr. Speaker. A statute of Henry VIII, dating back to 1512, refers to "the-dominion honours". In 1688 a new commission in Britain was issued to Governor-Sir Edmond Andros including within "the dominion of New England both New York and the Jerseys." The word "dominion" was then plainly synonymous with colony, plantation and possession. It certainly cannot be said that New York at that time was not in the constitutional position of a colony, yet it was called a dominion.
In Webster's international dictionary we find that the word "dominion" is defined as:
That which is subject to sovereignty or control. Territory governed, or over which authority is exercised.
In Funk and Wagnalls dictionary we find the word "dominion" defined as:
Obedience, servitude, slavery, subjection, subjugation, submission.
I hold in my hand the Winston dictionary published in Toronto as late as 1945 and I find that the word "dominion" is defined asr
A territory or country with a high degree of local' authority, but subject to the control of another government; as the Dominion of Canada.
In the British North America Act, section 3, it is stated:
The provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick shall form and be one dominion under the name of Canada.
Section 5 enacts that not the Dominion of Canada but Canada shall be divided into four provinces, namely, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. In section 4 appears the following: the name "Canada" and not "Dominion of Canada". It also says:
The name "Canada" shall be taken to mean "Canada," as constituted under this act.
The generic term "government of Canada"' is to be found in sections 11, 12, 13, 16, 116,. 118, 132, 142 and 145. The expression "parliament of Canada" not "parliament of the dominion of Canada" is to be found in sections 17, 18, 19, 20, 35, 40, 41, 47, 51, 52,. 58, 90, 92, 94, 95, 100, 101, 105, 120, 130, 131, 132, 133, 136, 141 and 146.
Section 22 refers to chapter I of the Consolidated Statutes of Canada. The great seal' of Canada is mentioned in sections 34, 35, and 38. House of Commons of Canada is; referred to in sections 87, 101 and 128. Therefore I contend that the official name of our country is not and never has been "Dominion of Canada" as is generally believed but "Canada" only. The word "dominion" was used only for the purpose of stating the constitutional position. It was recognized!

British North America Act in 1867 that the new constitution did not constitute Canada a sovereign state. It was to remain in the position of a colony with a certain degree of self-government and of dependence. It was then merely a matter of deciding what term should be used to describe that position and the term "dominion" was selected.
Our Conservative friends are silent tonight, but there were bursts of protest-
