subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
We
must recognize that Canada has gone a long way toward full political maturity when the leaders of all the parties in this chamber agree on the advisability of the country having full
'Mr. Arsenault.]

control over its constitution. For the government party, the Liberal party, it is the logical sequence to its long stand on the question of full national autonomy. It is the ultimate of a long series of steps taken gradually to ensure or to manifest our complete sovereignty. It is one of the last milestones on our way from colonialism to nationhood. For the Conservatives, as I have no doubt their leader has been authorized to speak for his party, it is a new step that deserves due notice. It is, if not an entire reversal of attitude, at least an evolution in its approach to matters of an emancipative nature as far as our constitutional position is concerned. We are of course faced with an attempt to delay a measure long overdue but the objections are founded on a different basis than heretofore, and the principles invoked for the advisability of delaying this measure are not openly based on the traditional Conservative ground of imperial solidarity or fear of dissolution of commonwealth ties.
As to the C.C.F. party, its leader has been consistent with himself and with the views usually expressed by his supporters on that question. I must recognize that they have usually expressed the desire, which they seem to share with the Liberal party, of supporting all constitutional measures tending to bring about our complete emancipation and to eradicate anything which might permit some people to ignore or disregard our status as a sovereign nation. Therefore, sir, this debate, which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has heralded himself as one of the most significant since confederation, marks what I would like to consider as the dawn of a new era in Canadian politics, when all Canadians, no matter to which party they belong, have at last agreed on the necessity of thinking and acting first as Canadians and not in relation to their country's position in the commonwealth.
For too long Canada has been an orphan, so to speak, in the minds of many of its citizens. They have been at fault for diverse but regrettable reasons for too long a period. There were many Canadians whose ancestors came from the British isles who put the empire or Great Britain ahead of Canada in their hearts. For much too long a time also there have been many Canadians of French descent who have considered that their country ended at the limits of the province of Quebec. It has taken many years of patient preaching by nationally-minded Canadians of both racial groups to do away with that trend of thought. Today I think those who hold that obsolete and un-Canadian way of thinking are in the minority in both groups.

This resolution provides a way by which Canada may amend such parts of the British North America Act as concern those matters that come within federal jurisdiction. It does away with the possibility of anyone in this house tampering with the language and school rights already granted by the act of 1867. Its only effect is to put us in regard to our constitution in the same position as the provinces already are with regard to their constitutions, no more, no less.
I cannot see what danger there can be in this for the provinces and why they should be consulted except through their elected representatives in this house. This afternoon my colleague, the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage), asked a question of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) who had just completed his speech. The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet asked if it was not a fact that the first amendment to the constitution, which was made without consultation with the provinces, had been suggested by members of the then government who were the fathers of confederation. The hon. gentleman replied that that was so, but that because they were the fathers of confederation they represented directly the provinces. The fact is that they were acting as members of the Canadian parliament, just as we are. The present government is consulting the provinces through their elected representatives in this chamber.
I am of the opinion that we should go much farther than this resolution provides, that we should find ways by which Canada could enact a truly national constitution. Much has been said and agreed about the necessity of amending the constitution; little has been said about the necessity of proclaiming a truly Canadian constitution. I shall have more to say about this later on. I think the time has come to take the first step toward proclaiming a Canadian constitution, but I also think it will take time to accomplish that. In the meantime it is advisable that we should take the steps we are taking during the present session and set up a court of last appeal and assume the right already possessed by the provinces of amending the constitution in connection with such matters as are of our exclusive jurisdiction.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) rightly pointed out that, of the eleven amendments which had been made to the British North America Act, nine had to do only with federal matters and were made without any consultation with the provinces. The new procedure being proposed by the government would simply confirm what has been done in the past. It will provide a way of doing this which is more consistent with our national dignity.
British North America Act
As I said, it may take some time before Canadians may be able to agree on the terms of a constitution and in this regard I should like to refer to an article in a newspaper which I think all hon. members have seen. The headline reads:
We will never yield on B.N.A. Act-Duplessis
If before any discussions have been had, if before any meeting has been officially convened, one of the parties to that meeting declares that he will not do anything, that he will not co-operate or collaborate, what results can we expect from the conference? How long will it be before Canadians can agree on a constitution? But it is interesting to read, not only the headline, but what is reported to have been said by the premier of Quebec. If I may be permitted to say so, this is nothing but an appeal to parochialism and prejudice. This statement distorts the facts because nothing of what is mentioned here has ever taken place nor have the bogeymen that are brought forward in this declaration ever existed. The article goes on to say:
"This is not a matter between Duplessis and St. Laurent," the premier said. "It is a matter of life and death. This is the time to express our opinions."
"It is not a question of separatism or fanaticism, it is simply a question of patriotism, well understood," the Quebec premier said.
In spite of what he said I cannot find one argument by the premier of Quebec to show what he is afraid of. He just goes on to talk of the revolt of 1837, and I read from the report:
He told delegates that their ancestors had lived for years in a "state of semi-slavery, having nothing to say about their government, and the public moneys spent."
We have long passed that stage. There is no danger of anyone in any party or in any part of Canada wanting to put Quebec in that position. It is simply an effort to make a bogeyman out of nothing. It is simply an appeal to prejudice. The report continues:
He said they fought to obtain the right to elect representatives, and described the 1837 rebellion, which led, "after many efforts," to the Act of Union in 1840, which united Ontario and Quebec into one province.
No one wants to bring about that condition again. There is no one in this country who is uttering a word against the liberties or the rights of Quebec. They are not even mentioned. On the contrary, special effort is made in the resolution to exclude any rights which have been granted to the provinces. The resolution reads:
The amendment from time to time of the constitution of Canada, except as regards matters coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces-
There is no mention at all in the resolution of anything that would have any effect on

British North America Act provincial rights. This is simply taking a step in the right direction which, as I said a moment ago, I hope will be followed by the proclamation of a truly national constitution. There is nothing in this resolution that menaces the liberties or autonomy of the province of Quebec. According to this report the premier went on to say:
"The authors of confederation decided upon a government based on the rights of the pioneer provinces . . . They decided on many autonomous governments instead of a central government which would have assimilated the (provincial) legislatures."
No one wants to assimilate the legislatures. The fact is that we are protecting their rights by this resolution. The only judgment that we can form on such a declaration is that it is a political appeal for political reasons to try to get the people of Quebec to find in Mr. Duplessis the defender of their rights. The province of Quebec knows now that it has at the head of the country and at the head of the Liberal party a man who will respect the rights of Quebec as much as those of all other provinces of Canada. We have had enough of such appeals to prejudice in this country. How can we expect harmony to come out of the next constitutional convention, the next dominion-provincial conference, when a man comes forward before he knows anything about what will be proposed at that conference and says: We will not do anything; we are in danger. It is just a plain farce for political reasons.
In the past the Liberal party, Mr. Speaker, has stood strongly in this house as well as in the provincial legislatures as the defender of provincial autonomy, long before Duplessis or people of his kind ever existed. But the Liberal party also stands as the defender of national autonomy, sovereignty and unity in Canada.
In introducing the measure the government's first consideration evidently is to do away with the necessity of going to another country for the amendment of provisions that concern only the federal powers. If the provinces had to come to Ottawa or to Westminster for amendments affecting their own prerogatives they would be the first to object to it and to claim their right of disposing themselves of their own privileges and prerogatives. Therefore there is no basic danger to any provincial rights in the present measure.
The strongest objection is that the government is proceeding piecemeal with its reform of our constitutional machinery, and that is quite so. I can see no cause for alarm in this but a determined effort to effect, when the moment is ripe and when public opinion favours it, the necessary changes that will affirm further our full autonomy and our
[Mr. Pieard.J

national sovereignty, instead of waiting for the pleasure of a man like Duplessis to agree to the necessary measures. It is all very well to say that because Westminster will accept any change we ask for it is sufficient proof of our autonomy. Yet it is anomalous to have to put in motion this cumbersome machinery each time we want to act in our own right within the realm of our federal powers, and when the provinces can exercise their own prerogatives freely and alter the use or disposal of their rights within the powers given to them by the confederation act.
This afternoon the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), in a very eloquent speech, mentioned many Canadian statesmen and quoted at one time the Hon. Mr. Mercier, a former premier of the province of Quebec, who had stated that the existence of the provinces preceded that of the dominion, and that it was from the provinces that the powers of the federal government were derived. He said that they are sovereign in the limits of their attributions. We do not deny that. It is our contention that the provinces are sovereign within the limits of their powers. Elies sont souveraines dans les limites de leurs attributions. That is what we contend also. We do not want to alter any of those powers without a conference.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said that a conference will be called, and it must be for the purpose-although I am not in on the secret-of elucidation on the necessary changes that may affect some rights that are borderline rights or that are provincial rights. In this resolution, however, where we are dealing with our own prerogatives, nothing is proposed that would force the government to appeal to the provinces. None of the authorities that my friend quoted this afternoon apply to the present situation. We are not affecting provincial rights nor any of their prerogatives in any way. We do not want to alter or diminish any of their rights. By voting for the resolution we do not contradict in any way the views of previous leaders which applied to material changes in the rights of the provinces. That is what they meant.
I do not believe that the present Prime Minister, any more than any other hon. member, would want to infringe on the rights of the provinces without their consent or without a normal agreement having been arrived at. We do not endanger in any way the rights given to the provinces under section 133 of the British North America Act, as my friend suggested. On the contrary we certify them; we specify that we shall not have the right to make changes affecting schools and languages.

As to the fields where both sides may consider that they have rights, they can do as has been done in the United States or in any other confederation. They can go to the courts of justice to have them judged, and I think it is quite unfair to say that because the supreme coiirt judges are appointed by the central government they will be biased. It is an insult to our judiciary and to the minds of our legal men. As I said in a previous debate, these people do not stand as arbiters. They are judges and they will judge the law as well as, and probably much better than, members of the privy council, and as well as the Supreme Court of the United States does for United States laws.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said at one time that no question of sovereignty was involved. Nevertheless he is too good a lawyer not to be conversant with international law, and he later recognized that the necessity of going to another country for amendments is a reminder of our colonial era that no self-respecting nation ought to endure any longer. He differed in his opinion on the question of when it should be done, who should be consulted, and in what way, but it is hopeful for the future to see that he agreed on the necessity of doing away with that procedure.
To my mind the present measure, and that which abolished appeals to the privy council, were long overdue affirmations of our national sovereignty, but they can be considered as the last moves we can take before we launch a truly national campaign for complete constitutional emancipation by way of a Canadian constitution proclaimed in Canada.
I am perfectly in accord on this question with the proposal that the leader of the opposition made at one time that a national constituent assembly be summoned, although I thought it was perhaps a way of delaying action. I am in accord that it should be the ultimate aim, but from what I showed the house a moment ago it would take a long time to come. I think we all should have as our aim that Canada should have its own constitution.
I should like to quote what I said on the matter on the 11th of June, 1946, in the debate on the redistribution bill. I stated:
Canada has outgrown her outmoded, colonial style constitution, and it is time lor her to assert her national will and to take her place among those nations of the world which have elaborated constitutional monuments as their basic law. Canada owes it to herself to nominate a constituent assembly and to draft a new constitution.
I think we can all agree on that when we see so many parties agreeing on the necessity of amending our constitution. There is only
British North America Act one step to go to realize that we should have a constitution that would not be the act of a foreign country.
The basis for a new constitution might well be, and probably should be, the British North America Act, but it need not be a full repetition of it nor a rehash, if I may say so, of its contents. When I say it should be the basis I mean that the religious, language and school rights granted by the British North America Act should not be tampered with and should not be diminished in any way or form. I mean that the division of power as between the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures should not be altered without agreement; but it would be useless to go to all that trouble if we were to repeat verbatim, of the British North America Act, what was suitable in 1867 but what may not be considered advisable in 1950. Yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) pointed to many clauses that would not be consistent with our status of today. If I am not mistaken he mentioned sections 55, 56 and 57, and quite aptly. There may be many others which we call spent clauses, that are of no further use and which should not be continued. Furthermore there are many conventions, precedents and grants of privileges by the former so-called mother country that have become part of our constitutional heritage and which, where applicable, might well be included in the new instrument. Referring to Ollivier on "Problems of Canadian Sovereignty", at page 44 the author says:
We generally look upon our constitution as being a written constitution because it is to be found in the British North America Act, but here again this statement is only partly true, for it is correct to say that our constitution is also partly unwritten as it "includes all the great landmarks of British and Canadian history as well as generally recognized conventions and usages."
Speaking in 1946-and this may please the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker)-I said:
... I personally would include in the constitution not only the provisions of the British North America Act but such an act as was suggested some time ago by the hon. member for Lake Centre, namely, a bill of rights, which should be part of our constitution.
Since that time the United Nations have drawn up such a bill of rights, much of which could be included in our constitution. Many of the countries emancipated after the first great war have such provisions in their constitutions. I have several before me, and it seems strange that I should pick up the constitution of Turkey, in which country many democratic rights may not be fully respected; but that constitution provides:
All Turks are equal before the law and are, without exception, obliged to respect it . . .
Natural rights of Turks include: inviolability of person, liberty of conscience, of thought, of speech,

British North America Act
of publication, of travel, of contract, of work, of possession, the liberty of association and assembly, and to form commercial societies.
That is just one of many such constitutions; and I think that would be an advisable thing for us to consider when a national convention meets. The full sovereignty of the country should be proclaimed, and the democratic character of our form of government should be emphasized. When we think that there is nothing in the terms of the British North America Act to outline even the responsible form of the government that is ours, it is clear that such a declaration should be included in the constitution, because much was left unsaid in 1867.
Referring to the British North America Act we find a description of the executive council; then in section 48 it is provided that questions arising in the house shall be decided by a majority. These are the only references to confirm the fact that we have rule by majority and that we have a democratic form of government; nothing is stated directly. Britain's constitution cannot be found in one instrument, and it is thus called unwritten. But it has its source in many historical documents such as Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights, and innumerable precedents and laws that have sanctioned the evolution of constitutional customs. I doubt whether for a federal state like Canada it would suffice to re-edit the British North America Act and rest upon British customs and precedents.
We are a mature nation. It may be that economically, as some maintain, our part of the continent might have fared better had we become united with the thirteen states that formed the nation to the south in 1774. But our destiny has unfolded otherwise. We have evolved through a slow process into a separate and independent unit, no matter what may be the views of many as to what would have been our fate had we cut the ties with Britain when the other colonies did. That is useless speculation and wishful thinking. Now we must all play our part in the continuing evolution of our institutions toward full manifestation of our undeniable rights as a sovereign nation. We are a mature people, and our constitution should be the mirror of our enlightened conception of a young, modern and energetic state. The childish contentment at having grown out of our former constitutional shackles should not express itself in the copying of institutions which may have suited another country in other years. There is no immutable form of constitution, any more than there is an 
immutable form of government. As John Hawgood says in his book "Modern Constitutions since 1787":
. . . while certain individual constitutions might seem particularly admirable, no one type of ideal state could suit all conditions of people and all environments.
It would be folly to tie ourselves to a too rigid constitution; yet it would not suit our federal form of government to have a vague system of precedents and customs and conventions in a constitution loosely knit around a symposium of the principles of the British North America Act. It might not suit us either geographically or ethnically.
We need a really well defined constitution which will recognize our position in the world of today and will contain provision for amendment according to the needs of tomorrow, while safeguarding the sacred rights which are one of the bases of our unity in diversity. Several hon. members have quoted the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. I should like to put on record a statement he made in a lecture delivered in Montreal on January 16, 1932:
A constitutive agency, whatever it may be, agreed to unanimously by the citizens of a state, ought not to prevent the future modification of the regime which it established. Sovereignty is inalienable and imprescriptible, and one generation has not the metaphysical right to bind definitely the future generations and to remove from them the competence which they themselves have used. It cannot determine beforehand and in an absolute manner the kinds of political and social realities of the future. The reforms ought to be made difficult but not impossible. Their realization ought to be subject to forms, procedures and to delays, but when a constitutional reform is demanded by the political or social situation of a country, and desired by a great majority of its citizens, prohibitions enacted twenty years, fifty years or a hundred years before should not constitute an obstacle. They will then be either violated or turned around.
That is a statement by a gentleman who has been quoted frequently during this debate. It is strange how our friends make heroes and gods of our great men after they are dead, but do not recognize them when they are alive.
The modern constitutions owe much to the development of thought since the publication of Montesquieu's l'Esprit des Lois and the great words of the French encyclopaedists whose preachings have opened the way for recognition of the equality of men, of their rights and for the reshaping of constitutional institutions throughout the world. It is true that most modern constitutions, up to the new constitution given to Italy by Mussolini in 1920, have taken their inspiration from the French constitution of 1793.
There is one thing we are prone to overlook, however, and that is that if it is true that the United States is one of the young

countries with regard to its period of existence, it is equally true that its constitution is one of the oldest of the democratic constitutions in the world. The constitution of the United States has also had a considerable influence on constitutional development throughout the world. It might not be inadvisable, therefore, to have a close look at it without intending to be any more servile in that direction than we ought to be in exactly copying the British customs.
The Prime Minister has let us know, Mr. Speaker, that a dominion-provincial conference will take place following this session. I wonder if this would not be the time to devise a means of forming a constituent assembly and to arrive at an agreement on the formation of a drafting committee charged with the task of formulating a truly Canadian constitution. I believe from what we hear of the feeling in certain quarters, no attempt should be made to discuss the details of the constitution or its amendments at that dominion-provincial conference. Instead of that, there should be a general discussion of the aims and purposes of a constituent assembly, the ways to compose it and the methods by which it might work. I think perhaps the drafting committee ought to be limited to, let us say, sixty members and made up of an equal number for both the dominion and the provinces. I agree with the leader of the C.C.F. party in his opinion that the committee should be composed of the different parties so that the various trends of thought in the country could be represented. Such a committee could study the problem and hear from the different constitutional authorities as to the things which should be included in the constitution.
This committee should, in turn, submit an agenda to the provinces and have those provinces submit a proposed draft constitution. After a period of about three months for the provinces to consider the matter, a meeting should be held to work out compromises on certain sections in the various draft proposals. After a final draft has been arrived at, it might be sent to the provinces for their consideration. They might be given, let us say, two months to consider that. After this committee had explored the whole situation, the convention itself might be summoned and the question studied there on its merits.
Any question arising on something in the draft should be settled only in a manner which meets with the approval of two-thirds of the delegates. My idea of the constituent assembly is that it would be a very large body of people and would 'nclude all the members of the federal par1 lament, as well as an equal number from f fl the provinces.
British North America Act Care would be taken to provide representation for the various trends of opinion based on the last election. If a province normally has ninety-eight seats and should send only seventy-seven people, it should not select seventy-seven from one party but a fair representation from all parties.
After this convention has carefully considered the situation, it might arrive at an agreement. The meetings of the committee should be in camera. There should be no publicity so we would avoid having the committee used as a platform for political purposes. Real work could be accomplished in such a committee before a constituent assembly is summoned- Worth-while suggestions could be studied by such a body and then submitted to an assembly of Canadian statesmen. This is just an idea of mine, but I believe it might be worth exploring.
The methods of amending that constitution would also of necessity be more elaborate than those which we find in most countries. I have not enough time to go into the details, but most modern states provide for a limited number of people to vote in one house before the constitution can be changed. It may need a two-thirds vote or a three-fifths vote.
In Canada today each of the provinces has the right to amend its constitution. I should think that in the new constitution there should be a provision to the effect that even in those legislatures, a two-thirds vote would be necessary before a change could be made. The same provision should be made applicable to changes with regard to the powers of the federal parliament. A two-thirds vote of the members of this house should be necessary. These rights the provinces already have and the federal parliament will have after this resolution is passed.
There would remain for consideration the minority rights, and I would think they could easily be safeguarded by making it necessary before any change is made in such matters to have it approved by two-thirds of the members in the federal house and by two-thirds of the members in the legislature of all of the provinces. I do not think we should fear any danger if such a provision were enacted. In any form of Canadian constitution, Mr. Speaker, provincial autonomy should not be violated, but the structure of our constitution should not be such as to weaken the nation as a whole. Canada cannot safely develop into separate units fighting against each other over the taxpayers' necessary contributions. The best methods should be devised whereby all governments, federal and provincial, may operate efficiently with a minimum burden on the citizens.
Complications can originate only in the minds of fearful people and also in the minds

British North America Act of political Machiavellis such as we now have at the head of the provincial government of Quebec.
The jurisdictional clauses of the constitution cannot extend to more than two classes of legislative authority, the federal and provincial. The latter already have the right to amend their constitutions. Once the measure now before us is passed, the federal parliament will have a right to amend the constitution in connection with matters falling within its jurisdiction. There would remain only those minority rights I mentioned a moment ago, school or religious rights. As I have explained, those could be safeguarded the same way. Only when we have achieved such a constitutional structure with clear-cut provisions for amending it, can we hope to take this problem out of the field of political speculation and political squabbling.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention the amendment that was proposed by the C.C.F. group. I do not think there is any danger that this government or any other government might want to extend its life; yet this amendment deserves consideration. I would think twice before I would vote against it. The amendment states that-
... as regards the requirement of section twenty of this act that there shall be a session of the parliament of Canada at least once each year, or as regards the requirement of section fifty of this act that no House of Commons shall continue for more than five years.
I believe that is a sound parliamentary principle. Whether or not I vote for this amendment, I believe our future constitution should definitely and clearly settle that question. I consider that amendment a valuable contribution to the debate.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I firmly believe the measure now before us is in the national interest. It violates in no sense the spirit of confederation, nor does it endanger the rights of the provinces or minorities. What more can be demanded, Mr. Speaker, until such time as we are in position to proclaim a truly national constitution, which I hope may be given to this country at the instigation of the present Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we in this house, the representatives of the people, are fortunate to be able to rise today and participate in a debate of such scope and importance on an act to amend the British North America Act, 1867, relating to the amendment of the constitution of Canada.
At the election held last June we were given a mandate by the people of our country; and it is a known fact today that all


Canadians were aware of the intention of our Liberal government at the next, the twenty-first, parliament to propose a bill enabling us to amend our own constitution. On June 27 the same people of Canada gave those who advocated such a measure an overwhelming majority, thereby sanctioning the program that we have now decided to implement.
I will say here in this house that the people of my constituency-like those of a large number of other constituencies who have sent members here on the Liberal ticket -who have accepted my platform, which is the Liberal platform, have given me a majority vote well aware of our intention regarding this amendment. I am here today by the will of my people because I am a supporter of the present Liberal government of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent); and it is my duty to support this bill proposed yesterday by our Prime Minister.
Two world wars and an intense participation in world affairs have placed Canada among the leading countries of the world. Yet our country, which we like to call "Land of hope and glory, mother of the free", is not yet free to amend its own constitution. Until that objective is achieved, it is impossible to call it a sovereign country. It is true that when a child learns to walk it needs a helping hand and a good deal of coaching. But I believe that we have now passed that stage and that we are ready to walk. Yet we still are obliged to rely on the government of another country for a solution to our legal problems.
To those who advocate protection of minority rights I wish to say that I, as a French-speaking Canadian, belong to that minority and that I certainly have no fear as regards the rights and privileges of the people of my race. I have great confidence in the decisions of our own supreme court; I am sure that those rights and privileges are in good hands and that they will be well protected whenever we shall have recourse to this legislative body.
Since the creation of the supreme court in 1875, no unfortunate decision has yet been attributed to that federal court of justice; and let me say here that this body will be in a better position than a body in another country to understand our needs and to render the best possible solution. Other countries of the commonwealth have tried the experiment, and I have yet to learn that one of them regrets having taken such steps. Since 1900 Australia has been master of its own decisions. South Africa followed the example in 1909, and New Zealand has already taken a step in that direction.

Evolution is unavoidable. We have progressed in the art of governing ourselves since the British North America Act of 1867, which followed the Quebec Act of 1774, the Constitutional Act of 1791 and the Act of Union of 1841. We have now in 1949 to decide, by the present bill, to give our own supreme court power to amend our constitution. Let it be understood, sir, that such amendments will pertain solely to questions of a federal scope; and you may rest assured that the people of Canada will never tolerate our meddling in the affairs of the provinces. We ask from the parliament of Westminster this right, and nothing else.
Some hon. members will hold that it would be preferable to consult the provinces before going into such an enterprise. I am at a loss to see anything wrong in this attitude of ours which is, first, to secure the right to amend our constitution and then to consult the provinces as to the ways and means of doing so. Why not start with the first thing first, and with one question at a time? We have tried to do otherwise before, and the result has been a lamentable failure.
No hon. member in this house is against the idea of first establishing our sovereignty, which right we have certainly acquired through our participation in world conflicts and in our co-operation in the settlement of world affairs. When we have taken that step, we can consult the provinces on the next logical problem to be solved, namely, the amendments to the constitution which are in the best interest of the ten provincial governments. A man of outstanding sagacity has set forth the axiom of the art of governing with a precision that has never erred. Junius, the great legislator, said:	"Eternal vigilance
is the price of liberty." And with Sir Wilfrid Laurier I will add:
The cabinet form of government lends itself marvellously to this necessary vigilance. On one side of the house you have those who govern and on the other side, those who watch.
As we shall most likely always work under the cabinet form of government, I will say, sir, that there will always be two sides; one to administer and to amend, and the other to watch; both sides, as a whole government, endeavouring to give to the country the best possible administration. One good way to achieve this aim is to secure this right to amend our constitution.

Mr. Speaker, although I approved the principle of amending the constitution mentioned during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I must, in fairness to myself and to the principles advocated, oppose the resolution as it now stands. No
British North America Act one denies that the constitution must be amended since it does not fully comply with our needs; however, as I support the theory that the constitution is a pact, a treaty, a convention rather than mere legislation I cannot admit that the present government has the right to decide arbitrarily and of its own accord what rights come under dominion jurisdiction on the one hand, and provincial jurisdiction on the other.
The whole country is wondering why the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) feels impelled to take the place of all the great jurists in order to impose his own personal views. I am not loath to state, in the wake of the premier of Quebec-even though my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) starts at the very sound of this name-that:

Mr. Speaker, I shall not intervene in this debate at any great length because it has been going on for some time and most of the ideas that could be developed have been developed. However, I should like to say a few words about the so-called compact or contract theory of confederation. As luck would have it, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche), who just preceded me, stated certain opinions on this subject with which I beg to differ.
The hon. member said that our constitution is a pact or contract, but I submit that it is not. I intend to develop my argument by showing that it could not be a contract or a pact because a contract must take place between existing parties who have the legal capacity to contract, and there must be some understanding. That is elementary in law and I intend to develop those three points briefly.
Before I do so I should like to say to the hon. member for Labelle that he is greatly mistaken when he says that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has taken it upon himself to impose his views on the subject of confederation upon those of the majority of well known jurists. Anyone who has studied the question must know that this matter has been debated back and forth for many years. There are two schools of thought. One school holds that confederation is a statute while the other school holds-this is the school of thought followed by the hon. member-that it is a contract. Nearly all the constitutional authorities now accept the theory that it is not a pact, that it is not a contract, but that it is a true statute.
I should like to refer to another argument advanced by the hon. member for Labelle. He says that the present government of Canada wishes to take away from the provinces the legitimate safeguards that were written into confederation by the fathers of confederation. Rather than taking away legitimate safeguards the government proposes to give to the minorities of this country, to give to the use of the French language and to give to the educational rights in this country, safeguards which have not existed under the constitution up to the present moment.
The hon. member for Labelle also said that the constitution of Canada as embodied in the British North America Act is based entirely on the resolutions passed at Quebec. He quoted Sir John Macdonald as having
said that those resolutions had to be adopted in their entirety. Any student of constitutional law or of the history of our country knows that, far from being based on the resolutions of Quebec, the British North America Act actually embodied less than half of those resolutions while it embodied a good deal of additional material inserted in it by the British parliament at the time it was passed. In substance it is a statute of the British parliament and is not, as has been stated many times, based entirely upon the resolutions passed by the colonies before confederation became a fact.
For confederation to be a pact it would have to be a pact between existing contracting parties. At the time the British North America Act was passed the Dominion of Canada did not exist; it came into existence only as a result of the legislation passed at that time. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec did not exist; at that time they were united under the Act of Union. While Prince Edward Island existed at that time it did not enter confederation until some time later under an agreement. British Columbia came in afterward under an agreement. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta were created by the dominion parliament. None of those provinces existed at that time. The Dominion of Canada, with which they are supposed to have contracted, did not exist either.
My second point is that they did not have the legal capacity to contract. The colonies that existed at that time were not part of the dominion and did not have the legal capacity to make treaties with one another to form a federal state. It was not done in that way. It was done by an address to the British parliament which was the only legislative body that had the power to create the Dominion of Canada. That was done by a statute of the British parliament and not by any pact or understanding. As I have said, the parties to that so-called pact did not exist and, in the second place, they did not have the capacity to contract.
My third point is that in fact there was no agreement which became the basis of confederation. It is easy to establish this by going back into constitutional history and looking at the so-called Quebec resolutions. If you examine those and the British North America Act which was passed subsequently you will see that there was no such agreement. The supposed agreement upon which those who advocate the compact theory rely was never incorporated into the British North America Act. Things were deleted and other things were added. It was not at all the same thing, not at all the same understanding.

In 1935 a committee of this house was created to consider whether confederation was a pact or contract. Some of the greatest constitutional authorities in Canada gave evidence before that committee, including Dr. Beauchesne, who was clerk of this house for so long. I am sure hon. members of this house have the greatest admiration for his learning and knowledge of constitutional law. All the constitutional authorities who gave evidence at that time before the committee were of the opinion that the British North America Act was in truth a statute and was not in any sense a pact or contract. It has been said that certain of our political leaders and writers have said that it is a pact and have used the word "pact" or the word "contract" when talking about confederation. I say, with all respect for those who have used those expressions, that they were not speaking from a strictly legal point of view. In this house we are a legislative body. Our purpose is to legislate and we are commonly known as legislators. Therefore I submit we must look at these matters from a legal point of view.
I have pointed out that the constitution of Canada, from a legal point of view, is not based on a pact or a contract. If these people used the word "pact" or the word "contract" they did so for sentimental or political reasons, or possibly as a figure of speech in order to make a comparison. It may be said that although it is not a legal contract there was a moral understanding between the two great races that constituted Canada at that time, but that is as far as we can go. We may say that there was a gentleman's agreement, a sort of pacte d'honneur, as one would say in French, between the French and English speaking races at that time with respect to one another's rights and privileges. That is as far as we can go. We cannot say that it is in truth a pact or contract.
My conclusion is that, as the constitution is neither a pact nor a contract, our opponents, who base their arguments for safeguarding the rights of minorities, the right to use the French language, and educational rights on the theory that it is a pact or contract, are basing their arguments on very slippery ground, to put it mildly, on very dangerous ground. They are building on sand because they are basing their arguments on sentimental or political grounds but not on a sound legal basis. I say that after the legislation that the government is introducing has been introduced, after our constitution has been amended, and after the resolution has been implemented, then the rights pertaining to education, the use of the French language, and the protection of minorities in general

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take up only a few minutes of the time of this house in order humbly to set out my views on the point at issue.
The question is to know if henceforth this country may amend its own constitution, without first obtaining permission from a foreign power. I hope that this phrase, foreign power, will not be taken in a disparaging sense.
It would seem that all here are agreed that Canada should have this power.
But the point on which our opinion is not that of several members of this house is, no doubt, the manner in which this change must be effected.
I think I may, indeed must, expose at this juncture an old theory, even though it might appear somewhat contradictory to several hon. members, whose authority I respect since most of them, being lawyers, are admittedly superior to myself. The soundness of this theory has been contested, it seems, by many.
Everyone is entitled to his own opinion in this matter. I shall have the fullest respect for any who oppose my views, and I only ask for the same fairness in return, so long as I deal with this matter with due frankness and dignity. Even though the idea may seem antiquated, I shall try to prove to this house that the confederative act is a contract, and one that cannot be amended without the unanimous consent of the contracting parties.
Every member of this house is aware of the events which brought about in this country the discussions, meetings and negotiations which led to the Charlottetown and Quebec conferences. At that time two groups in Canada controlled all political and economic life: Upper Canada, inhabited mainly by Canadians of British origin, and Lower Canada, inhabited almost exclusively by Canadians of French origin.
Needless to add, these two groups displayed a rivalry which was exceedingly harmful to their normal individual development and to the harmony which should exist between citizens of the same country.

For a time it was thought that the Act of Union in Canada, passed in 1841, would have solved the problem. Unfortunately it was not to be so, and it was only through the great ability and vast energy of a Canadian, Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine, that a possibly irreparable deterioration of the situation was averted.
Fortunately the leaders of the two groups, both French and English, understanding that everybody's interest was at stake, decided to attempt the impossible in order to arrive at an understanding.
The discussions began. The great majority of the English leaders were in favour of a legislative union. On the other hand, the French ones held out for a confederative union. Concessions were made on both sides, but the province of Quebec was nevertheless allowed certain privileges which it was unwilling to sacrifice at any price and which it had indicated as essential conditions of its entry into confederation. After study, discussions, concessions from both sides, an agreement was finally arrived at and consent freely and mutually given to a formula. It is that agreement that we call a compact.
Who, may I ask, Mr. Speaker, is better qualified to give the exact name to the act they brought about than the very authors of this agreement? Can it be thought for a single moment that these gifted and well meaning men, the pick of the two races concerned, did not know the nature of the act which they brought about? Well, what name did they give it? All agreed to call it a contract, a treaty. I have collected several quotations, but shall not read them to the house.

The years went by. The parties to the treaty got used, more or less, to the yoke they had submitted to, of their own free will.
In 1907, a matter was brought up which reopened the discussion on the nature of the political constitution of Canada. A provision was being introduced to increase federal grants to the provinces.
What were the views expressed by the statesmen of that time? I shall give only two quotations from many that have been gathered.

British North America Act
In the Debates of 1906-1907, page 2199, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said during a discussion on legislation providing for an increase in the grants to the provinces:
Confederation is a compact, made originally by four provinces, but adhered to by all the nine provinces which joined the union.
And on the same page, Sir Robert Borden is reported as saying:
I agree with what has been said by the right hon. gentlemen regarding the undesirability of lightly amending the terms of our constitution-although of course all the provinces are represented here. But inasmuch as it is a federal compact which we are asked to vary . . .
Then more recently, in 1925, a full debate took place in this house on a resolution quite similar to the one before us now.
Let us review briefly what was said then by our statesmen, by our great party leaders who, after all, were as able as we are to appreciate events which were closer to them by some twenty-five years.
I wish to quote from page 332 of the Hansard of February 19, 1925, where the Right Hon. Mackenzie King stated the following:
Due regard should be had to the view that a compact was made at the time of confederation, and that an amendment of the importance that such an amendment certainly would have, ought only to be proposed after there had been a conference and agreement between the dominion and the provinces.
According to page 335 of Hansard of February 19,	1925, the Right Hon. Arthur
Meighen said:
Undoubtedly, the pact of confederation is a contract and there are rights involved therein not represented by the parliament of Canada . . . The speech of the Minister of Justice determines, I think, without power of dispute, that there should never be suggestion of amendment affecting other parties to the contract save after conference and consent of those other parties.
I shall now quote the opinion of the hon. Senator Thomas Vien, who must enjoy much consideration since he has been so well rewarded. Here is what he had to say on February 19, 1925, as recorded on page 310 of Hansard for that year:
I fully agree with the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that a pact which was entered into at a conference where all the component parts of what was then Canada were represented should not be lightly dealt with or amended, without a conference where the opinions of the representatives of all those provinces which now form part of the Dominion could be collected and fully considered.
And further on:
Our country is one of the contracting parties and no one can have the contract altered, except with the unanimous consent of the contracting parties.
[Mr. Poulin.1
And at page 313:
As in the case of a contract between private individuals, you cannot change the British North America Act without first convening a conference similar to that as a result of which the act originally came into being.
And the Hon. Ernest Lapointe expressed himself as follows, as reported in Hansard of February 18, 1925. I quote from page 298:
Now, has it (the Canadian constitution) been considered as a treaty? I heard it suggested some time ago that this idea at confederation of a treaty is an antiquated idea. Maybe it is. But, Mr. Speaker, truth does not cease to be truth when it gets old; an old truth is always true. You cannot prevent facts from being facts whether you like them or not.
Mr. Lapointe went on to say:
The British North America Act says itself that the Parliament of Great Britain merely enacted, put into a statute, the wish of the people of the provinces of Canada.
On that occasion, in 1925, there was scarcely an hon. member who did not agree in the house that confederation was a treaty.
And now, Mr. Speaker, all those opinions are worthless. We must forget all that. What was true yesterday no longer holds today. Everything has changed, everything has altered. Yet there are things that remain unchanged.
What has happened during the past twenty-five years to give a different aspect to historical facts?
Faced with the pressing needs of the second world war, we doubtless acquired the habit of compromising in a way we should never have countenanced in different circumstances.
It may be claimed that the theory of a constitutional compact has often been disregarded and, on such occasions, no objection was raised by the very people who are now protesting. In this respect, those whose duty it is to watch over the interests of the provinces are perhaps blameworthy, but the argument cannot justify anyone in perpetuating the evil done and still less in setting it up as a system.
I have the deepest respect for the Prime Minister. I think very highly of his personality and of the great office he fills with such distinction. On September 23,	1949, as
reported at page 196 of Hansard of the same date, he stated the following in the house:
The leader of the opposition says that whenever there has to be any kind of amendment whatsoever to any part of the constitution there should be consultation with the provinces. That is an opinion that is very frequently voiced, but it is one which we cannot accept. It would imply that the British North America Act is a contract . . .
With that theory we are in diametric disagreement.

And yet, on February 18, 1925, another great Canadian, Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, also a Quebec representative, made the following statement in the house, as reported in Hansard:
If the British North America Act is the charter of the provinces as well as the charter of the dominion, I ask again, how can we alter it without communicating with the provinces? . . . Would it be fair to take upon ourselves the right of amending this legislation which is the constitution of the provinces as well as our own?
On page 301:
They cannot be made arbitrarily; they cannot be made only at will and at the request of the dominion parliament; but those who are just as much interested as the dominion parliament in this matter must have their say, must be consulted and must give their assent.
And further on, on [DOT]the same page:
To those who want changes I would say that the only way to get them is the constitutional way to ask the consent of the various parties to confederation.
Mr. Speaker, since so many Canadians of sound judgment, so many experienced statesmen have always considered confederation to be a contract, let us at least give the contracting parties the opportunity to meet, to discuss, to try to agree in order that, unanimously, a new statute or a revised statute be introduced, in which, undoubtedly, the parties concerned will again have to accept some sacrifices, just as they did in 1867. It has been said that after this act was passed by the house, the provinces would be consulted and that, if a "satisfactory agreement" could be reached, an address would be presented to the parliament at Westminster.
It would be important to know, before this discussion ends, just what is meant by "satisfactory agreement".
Is it an agreement adopted unanimously by the provinces, such as that of 1867? If not, words and not powers will, in the future, form the bones of contention.
By satisfactory agreement do we mean exaggerated, even vexatious concessions, which the provinces will be practically compelled to accept, because, when faced with a fait accompli, they will be afraid to lose everything?
When referring to a fait accompli, I am obviously referring to the present act which will have been accepted by parliament and in which it will be nowhere specified that the unanimous consent of the provinces, or even of one of them, is required to amend our constitution.
I cannot believe for a moment, Mr. Speaker, that the prime motive of the movers of this resolution has been to have this legislation passed so that they might afterwards use it as a sword of Damocles at the provincial conference.

However, if such had been their objective,
I believe they could congratulate themselves on having very well succeeded.
On the other hand, I know quite well that the cause which the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) and I, along with many others in this house are upholding is a forlorn cause. In view of the huge majority the government has in this house, I do not make the mistake of thinking that our views will be accepted but when someone has decided to engage in a fight known to be hopeless, it is generally because he has also decided to hold fast to ideals which to him are sacred and immutable.
Granting this, Mr. Speaker, I now appeal to the Prime Minister's sincerity and good will, and I trust I shall not be deceived.
Far be it from me to think that the government and its leader want to sacrifice some of the inalienable rights which are granted to one or more groups, one or more provinces, in our beloved Canada. I believe we more likely differ on the procedure to follow in order to better ensure those rights.
Well, as the government will have the best of it, being in a position to make full use of the procedure it considers the most effective and which we deem dangerous, I would at least ask it to be careful, not to move too fast, mindful of the fact that the fathers of confederation took years and years to reconcile their minds towards an agreement.
I humbly suggest to the government, when the house has passed this legislation, to be very obliging, conciliating and patient with the representatives of the provinces who I understand are to be called to a conference. The government should give as much latitude as possible to the provinces, bearing in mind that the first Canadian constitution was drafted by the provinces, a historical fact that can never be gainsaid.
Mr. Speaker, I am not obstinate, I am not stubborn and if I could be useful to the government in its very difficult endeavour, I would offer my humble co-operation; but that, I know, is not necessary.
Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the individuals pass away rapidly, that generations follow as quickly and that the task we are undertaking today for their sake will be appreciated according to the earnestness with which we settle down to it.
However, since I cannot approve of the procedure followed by the government, I shall have to vote against the resolution.

I was suggesting however that, if it had been in order within the rules, this parliament would have had an opportunity of voting on a matter that is of preeminent interest to the people of this country as a whole. I made it clear at the beginning that there was no suggestion that you could have done otherwise than you did, having regard to the rule you invoked. I take it that the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard), with his close relationship to the previous minister of justice and his senior position in this house, must have been speaking for his party when he spoke of the necessity of the convening of such a national constitutional convention with a view to arriving at the means of amending our constitution. That statement was indeed interesting. By this procedure we are today laying the foundation in part for future amendments of this constitution.
We believe that the Prime Minister should have carried out the undertaking he gave when he spoke on the radio on May 19 last. At that time there was no circumscription which would in any way allow him to proceed in the manner in which he has proceeded in moving an address that provides only for parliament having the power to amend those things that are peculiarly within the federal jurisdiction.
I shall read his promise. If he and his party received a mandate, that mandate was with regard to something about which there never was any dispute, namely, that there is indeed need of amending the constitution in order to meet changed and changing conditions. No political party in this country, in the last fifteen years, has at any time enunciated a policy that denied the necessity for amendments to the British North America Act, subject of course to the protection of the rights of minorities, school rights and the like. But subject to those things, it has been agreed

that a means must be established of amending the constitution. I ask the Prime Minister, when he speaks, to answer one question. Where in this country did he say:	If my
party is returned to power, we will amend the constitution in a dual way; we will secure for parliament immediately the right to amend the federal portions of the constitution and then a little later on we will convene an assembly of dominion and provincial representatives with a view to arriving at a method of amending the constitution in its entirety. Here is the promise:
We Liberals also believe that a method should be worked out to amend our constitution in Canada.
That won't be easy.
We do not want the Canadian constitution to be too rigid, but we do want to make sure it contains the fullest safeguards of provincial rights, of the use of the two official languages, and of those other historic rights which are the sacred trust of our national partnership.
And this is the undertaking:
It is our intention, after the election, to consult the provincial governments with a view to working out a method, which will be satisfactory to all Canadians, of amending the constitution in Canada.
That, Mr. Speaker, was the undertaking given by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that he is so naive as to have believed that that was an undertaking by the party of which I was the leader to renounce the right that has been exercised for the last eighty-two years in this house, to have amended without consultation with the provinces those parts of the constitution that do not affect the jurisdiction of the provinces?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
The people of Canada must have been naive. The words of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) are incapable of any other interpretation, naivete or anything else to the contrary. The undertaking was given as well at Moncton. I could quote his exact words. He said that the government would seek provincial government co-operation in drafting ways and means of amending our constitution in Canada. He did not say that we would amend it piecemeal. He said "our constitution", not a part of our constitution, not a portion designated by the Prime Minister and those associated with him, but our constitution, which meant, and could only be understood to mean, the constitution of Canada without division. Some of us would like to know when the change came about and the reason for it.
There is no question whatsoever that there is almost unanimous opinion in this country
British North America Act as to the need of amendment. There has never been any question about that over the years. In 1925 the then prime minister of this country spoke of the need of amendment. The then minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe, spoke of the need of amendment. At that time Mr. Meighen spoke of the need of amendment. All of these men also stated the grave and difficult problems that would face any government that endeavoured to secure a general principle upon which amendment could be based.
There is no question that there is agreement in parliament and throughout the country as to the necessity of the protection of constitutional rights inherent in the constitution. There is no question that we wish to bring our constitution up to date in order to meet those changed and changing conditions which have occurred since 1867. May I go back beyond that and quote the words of Lord Brougham which indicate that he had a perception of the need of constitutional reform. He used these words:
Constitutions must grow if they are to be of any value: they have roots, they ripen, they endure. Those that are fashioned resemble painted sticks planted in the ground-they strike no root, bear no fruit, swiftly decay and ere long perish.
There is no argument about the necessity of amendment, but I think that, not in a party sense, not in a political sense but in a national sense, each of us in this parliament and in the country should do what the fathers of confederation did. They joined together. Many of them were personal enemies but they joined together for the purpose of achieving confederation. I feel that through a national constitutional convention we would be able to secure that measure of agreement, that measure of unanimity based on our pride as Canadians that would achieve a permanent and complete amendment of our constitution.
Before I go on I wish to refer to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). What a strange amendment it is! He believes that parliament should have the right to make the necessary amendments to the constitution in so far as the federal authority is concerned. In effect he says: "Give us that power". At the same time through this amendment he asks the British parliament to diminish the power of this parliament to do that which he says is so necessary to take a step in the direction of an amendment of our constitution. What a position this parliament will be in, going to Westminster and saying that we demand the power to amend our own constitution within the federal ambit of authority, then adding four lines at the end declaring that we do not want the power in so far as

British North America Act section 20 of the British North America Act is concerned. We want to ensure that the parliament of Canada will never deny a session every year and an election every five years.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Does the hon. member not agree?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: I agree with the necessity of such things being embodied in our constitution by precedent, but I do not agree that if we go to Westminster and ask for power we should at the same time say that we are afraid to trust ourselves in the years to come. As a matter of fact, by that amendment my hon. friend indicates that while he asks for that much he is afraid that if too much power is exercised by this parliament democracy is indeed in danger by reason of the amendment that he says he supports.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Will he say that the same condition applies to the English and French languages?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I must answer that question. I shall come to the question of compact, to which the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) referred. He said that there is no compact. In 1925 the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, called it a compact. In 1925 in the same debate Mr. Meighen referred to it as a compact. As far as constitutional rights are concerned, we in this party have always taken the stand that they are inviolable and are part and parcel of the basis upon which confederation was built.
On motion of Mr. Diefenbaker the debate was adjourned.
